question: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
options: Battle of Buxar - Mir Zafar vs Clive
Battle of Wandiwash - French vs East India Company
Battle of Chillianwala - Dalhousie vs Marathas
Battle of Kharda-Nizam vs East India Company
explanation: The decisive Battle of Buxar was fought in 1764 between the East India Company and combined forces of Mir Qasim, Shah Alam II and Shuja-ud-Daula. The combined forces had 40000 soldiers and the British forces had 18000 soldiers. The three separate allies could not coordinate in a better way and got defeated. The British won Battle of Buxar under the command of Major Hector Munro. After this battle, Shah Alam II surrendered to the British, Nawab Shuja-ud-Daula fled from the scene and took refuge to Rohilla and Mir Qasim also fled and died a few years later in extreme obscurity. Battle of Wandiwash was fought on January 22, 1760 between the army of the Brtitish East India Company (under the leadership of Sir Eyre Coote) and the French (under the leadership of Comte de Lally). The British forces under Sir Eyre Coote defeated the French in the Battle of Wandiwash and besieged Pondicherry. After the Battle of Wandiwash, the French capital of Pondicherry fell to the British in 1761 AD. The war was concluded with the signing of the “Treaty of Paris” of 1763 or the treaty of 1763 AD. As per terms of the treaty, the Chandranagar and Pondicherry was returned to France . The Battle of Chillianwala was fought in 1849 AD during the Second Anglo-Sikh War. Sikhs fought against British in this battle under Sher Singh. The Battle of Kharda took place in 1795 AD between the Maratha Confederacy under the Peshwa Madhavrao II of Maratha Empire and the Nizam of Hyderabad in which Nizam was badly de
source: IAS Pre G.S. 1995 · Modern India GS p.5

explanation: The First Carnatic War ended in 1748 when the Treaty of Aix-La Chapelle (October, 1748) was signed bringing the Austrian War of Succession to a conclusion. Under this treaty, first Carnatic war ended and France agreed to leave the Austrian Netherlands and gave back Madras to Britain in return for Louisbourg. Maria Theresa was also confirmed as Austrian ruler. It is significant that, between 1740 and 1748, most of Europe’s great powers were involved in a conflict caused by the question of Maria Theresa’s succession to the Austrian Habsburg crown. Thus, both statement 1 & 2 are correct.

Dupleix was called back at a crucial time
They conspired against the Indian powers
Their trading company was heavily dependent on the French Government.
explanation: The primary (fundamental) cause of French failure in India was that the French company was subject to excessive government control. Dupleix was handicapped in execution of his plans for need of funds and support from French government. There was an inherent weakness in the very nature of the organisation of the French Company. explanation: Regarding Anglo-Mysore Wars all statements are correct because the Anglo-Mysore Wars was a series of four military confrontations in India between the British and the rulers of Mysore. • Haidar Ali won the First Anglo-Mysore War (1767- 69), and the English was forced to conclude a very humiliating treaty with Haider Ali on April 4, 1769 - Treaty of Madras which brought an end to the War. • During Second Anglo-Mysore War (1780-84), on September 10, 1780, Tipu defeated Colonel Baillie's forces, which was the most humilating defeat ever suffered by the British at Indian soils. It is also known as Battle of Perambakkam. • Tipu Sultan was defeated in the Third Ango-Mysore War (1790-1792). The War ended with the Treaty of Srirangapatanam in 1792. • Tipu Sultan died in Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (1799) and all his treasures were confiscated by the British.
source: Gujarat PSC Pre-2018 Paper-I · Modern India GS p.9

question: Who among the following Governor-Generals formed the Triple Alliance against Tipu Sultan?
explanation: Haider Ali faced the Triple Alliance of the British, the Nizam and the Marathas in the First Anglo- Mysore War (1767-69). Hyder Ali using his diplomatic skills bought off the Marathas and won over the Nizam and thus broke the alliance. The war was brought to an end by signing of the Treaty of Madras in 1769. In 1782, Hyder Ali died in the course of the Second Anglo Mysore war and was succeeded by his son. In 1782, Tipu Sultan became the successor of Mysore Empire in the middle of a war. Tipu carried the Second Anglo Mysore War till 1784 when two sides concluded peace by signing the Treaty of Mangalore. In the Third Anglo Mysore War (1790-92), Tipu was defeated by the triple alliance of British, Nizam and Marathas which was formed by Lord Cornwallis and had to sign the Treaty of Seringapatam. In 1799, Tipu Sultan died at Srirangapatanam during Fourth Anglo-Mysore War.

question: Which one of the following statements about the Treaty of Allahabad is NOT correct?

Awadh was restored to its Nawab on payment of Rs. 50 Lakhs

explanation: The Treaty of Allahabad (16 August, 1765) was signed between Robert Clive, Shuja-ud- Daulah and Shah Alam II. As per the treaty, Awadh was returned to Shuja-ud-Daulah and his two districts Kara and Allahabad were taken away. He had to pay a war indemnity of Rs. 50 lakh to the Company. Awadh had been provided protection by the British. However, the Nawab would have to pay for the cost of the British troops. Hence Awadh acted as a buffer state between British-possessed Bengal and the Marathas. The districts of Kora/Kara and Allahabad and an annual pension of Rs. 26 lakh were given to Shah Alam II. In return, Shah Alam II granted Diwani rights of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa to the British. The Nawab of Bengal was made a puppet with no military or administrative powers. Varanasi was restored to Shah Alam-II on payment of certain amount of revenue to the Company.

question: First decisive military success of British East India Company in India is marked by—
explanation: The Battle of Buxar was fought on 22 October, 1764 between the forces under the command of the British East India Company led by Hector Munro and the combined armies of Mir Qasim, Nawab of Bengal till 1763, the Nawab of Awadh and the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II. The Battle was fought at Buxar, a small fortified town within the territory of Bihar, located on the banks of river Ganga. It was a decisive victory for the British East India Company. Shuja-ud-Daula and Shah Alam surrendered and the war was brought to an end by the ‘Treaty of Allahabad’ in 1765 AD. The Battle of Buxar established the company's dominance over Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. This war laid the foundation of British rule over Bengal along with the whole of India. Now there was no power left to demolish British empire. Thus the Battle of Buxar is regarded as the first decisive military success of British East India Company in India.

explanation: Siraj-ud-Daulah, the Nawab of Bengal, was annoyed from Britishers because they started the construction of Fort William at Calcutta without his permission and also misused the trading favors. question: The permanent settlement was rarely extended to other regions because-
options: increases in agricultural prices after 1810 increased the value of the harvest while the permanent settlement disallowed an increase in the State's share
the economic theories of Ricardo influenced the policy makers
the state found it expedient to settle directly with the ryot
explanation: The permanent settlement was rarely extended to any region beyond Bengal. After 1810 AD, there was a substantial growth in the income of zamindars because of the increasing value of harvest produced. The colonial state could not claim any share of this increased income as the revenue demand was fixed in perpetuity. Thus, in order to enlarge its financial resources, the colonial state left the idea of expanding Istamrari settlement. The colonial officials were under much influence of the ideas of David Ricardo, the renowned economist of the 19th century. He suggested that a landowner should have a claim only to the average rent prevailing at that time. According to him “when the land yielded more than this average rent, the landowner had a surplus that the state needed to tax. If tax was not levied, cultivators were likely to turn into rentiers and their surplus income was unlikely to be productively invested in the improvement of the land”. The British officials viewed the same condition had arisen in Bengal because of the introduction of istmarari settlement. Therefore they wanted to follow a different system of land revenue. Thus, the Ryotwari settlement of land revenue was introduced in Bombay Deccan. Due to these drawbacks it could not be extended to other regions of India. History of Modern India

explanation: The drain theory was put forward by Dadabhai Naoroji in his book ‘Poverty and Un-British Rule in India’. Sir Syed Ahmad Khan was loyal to British for the cause of Muslim upliftment. So, he did not believe in the drain theory of Dadabhai Naoroji.
source: IAS (Pre) G.S. 1996 · Modern India GS p.31

subject: AP & Indian History
question: The following items consist of two statements; Statement-I and Statement-II. Examine these two statements carefully and select the correct answer using the code given below: Statement I : Dadabhai Naoroji argued that what was being drained out was potential surplus" that could generate more economic development in India if invested in India Statement II : Imperialists believed that India was brought into the large capitalist world market and that was in itself a progress towards modernization
options: Both the statements are individually true and Statement II is the correct explanation of Statement I
Both the statements are individually true but Statement II is NOT the correct explanation of Statement I
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
explanation: The theory of Drain of Wealth" was primarily presented by Dadabhai Naoroji and he wrote a paper called "The English Debt to India”. According to him a large part of India’s national wealth or total annual product was exported to England for which the Indians got no adequate returns. Dadabhai Naoroji had said that the drain of wealth is the root cause of all evils and the main cause of Indian poverty. As a result of the drain of wealth, capital was not accumulated in India and the level of living continued to decline and poverty increased. Imperialists described this money extortion as fair. John Strachy thought that England gets the funds from India for better administrative system and establishment of law and justice. Thus both the statements are individually true but Statement-II is not the correct explanation of Statement-I.
source: UPSC CAPF G.S. Ist 2017 · Modern India GS p.31

subject: AP & Indian History
topic: Economic & social history of British India
question: Consider the following statements and select the correct answer from the codes given below the statements: Assertion [A]: Generally India had a favourable balance of trade during the British rule. Reason [R]: The drain of wealth took the form of unrequited exports. Codes:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
explanation: During British era the British economically exploited India by making a strategy. Instead of worrying about the people here, they forcefully imposed the economic policies on the Indians and their main aim was the interest of the British empire only. This exploitation policy totally paralyzed India's economic system. John Sullivan, the President of the Board of Revenue, Madras had wrote “Our system acts very much like a sponge, drawing up all the good things from the banks of Ganges and squeezing them down on the bank of the Thames”. The drain of wealth took the form of unrequited exports. Thus (A) is false and (R) is true.
source: UPPCS (Pre) G.S. 2017 · Modern India GS p.32

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Who of the following was/were economic critic/ critics of colonialism in India? 1. Dadabhai Naoroji 2. G. Subramania Iyer 3. R. C. Dutt History of Modern India 4 Select the correct answer using the code given below.
explanation: Dadabhai Naoroji, R. C. Dutt, Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Prithvi Chandra Roy, G.B. Joshi and G. Subramania Iyer were among those who grounded Indian nationalism firmly on the foundation of anti- imperialism by fashioning the world’s first economic critique of colonialism before Hobson and Lenin. Dadabhai Naoroji was the first such nationalist leader of modern India who exposed and certified the defective and deadly exploitation by the British rule of Indian economy through his articles in 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' (1901), ‘English Debt to India’, ‘The Wants and Means of India’ and ‘On the Commerce of India’ etc. The founder editor of ‘The Hindu’, G. Subramanyam Iyer also conducted economic analysis of colonialism through his newspaper. The author of the book, ‘Economic History of India,’ R. C. Dutt was a famous financial expert and he also made economic criticism of British colonialism.
source: IAS (Pre) G.S. 2015 · Modern India GS p.32

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Who had expressed the view that the ‘British Economic’ policy in India is loathsome?
explanation: Karl Marx had expressed the view that the British economic policy in India is loathsome. This will be the cause of social revolution in India. British interference having displaced the spinners in Lancashire and the weavers in Bengal are sweeping away both Hindu spinners and weavers, dissolved these small, semi-barbarian, semi-civilized communities by blowing up their economic basis and thus produced the greatest social revolution in Asia.
source: Uttarakhand UDA/LDA (Mains) 2007 · Modern India GS p.32

To develop a comprehensive scheme for Civil Services in India

explanation: There are several causes responsible for decline of textile industries in Bengal during 18th century- (i) High tariff on the goods exporting to Britain. question: Which of the following statement (s) is/are correct about de-industrialization? 1. This process started in 1813 2. The end of the trade union monopolies of the East India Company accelerated the process. Choose the correct answer from the code given below- Code:
explanation: As a result of the British rule in India, all the policies and programs of the Indian economy began to be formed in line with colonial interests. Since 1800 History of Modern India 4 AD, the Indian cotton industries were the most developed in the world. As a result of the industrial revolution, industrialization began in European countries and production began to grow simultaneously. But the de-industrialization started in India after that period. Due to Napoleon Bonaparte’s Continental System in Europe (which prohibited the import of British goods into French allies in Europe) the British traders and merchants suffered. So they demanded that they have to be given a share in the British trade in Asia and dissolve the monopoly of the East India Company. The company objected to this. Finally, British merchants were allowed to trade in India under a strict license system under the Charter Act of 1813. The degradation of traditional handicrafts industry in India resulted in the accumulation of British goods in Indian markets because Indian handicrafts could not compete with cheap British merchandise. So both statements are true.

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Economically, one of the results of the British rule in the 19th century was the
options: increase in the export of Indian handicrafts
growth in the number of Indian owned factories
rapid increase in the urban population
explanation: Economically the results of the British rule during the 19th century were as follows- (i) De-industrialization and decline of Indian handicraft industry. (ii) Growing poverty of farmers. (iii) The destruction of old landlords (Zamindars) and rise of the new landowner (Zamindari) system. (iv) Commercialization of Indian agriculture. (v) Development of modern industries. (vi) Economic development policies of British government led to famine and poverty. In the second half of the 19th century, there was an important change by commercialization in Indian agriculture. Prior to this, agriculture was a way of living and not a commercial commodity. During this period some special crops were produced for national and international markets, not for self use. The production of peanuts, sugarcane, jute, cotton, oilseeds, tobacco, spices, fruits and vegetables increased and in commercial areas like tea, coffee, rubber and indigo, commercialization of agriculture reached its climax. The benefits of commercialization of agriculture came to the middlemen but the farmers had no benefit. 08. Freedom

explanation: The Revolt of 1857 was a major uprising in India during 1857-58 against the British regime, but it was unsuccessful and was suppressed by the British East India Company. subject: AP & Indian History
question: Which one of the following upheavals took place in Bengal immediately after the Revolt of 1857?
explanation: The revolt of 1857 was followed by the Indigo Revolt started by the peasants of Bengal. This revolt was started from Govindpur village of Nadia district in Bengal, in 1859-60. The revolt was led by 'Digamber Vishwas and Vishnu Vishwas. The revolt was described in 'Patriot' the magazine edited by Harishchandra Mukherji and in 'Neel Darpan' a play written by Deenbandhu. It was the most broad and combative revolt among the peasant revolts which had taken place till then. The Peasants of Bengal who wanted to cultivate rice in their fields, were compelled to grow Indigo and in case of denying they would have to face brutal consequences of the Indigo planters. Indigo Commission issued a report on November 1860, stating that no ryots could be compelled to cultivate Indigo and all disputes would be settled by legal procedure. Major revolts and their timeline. Sanyasi Revolt 1770-1820 Kol revolt 1831-1832 Santhal Revolt 1855-1856 Indigo Revolt 1859-1860 Pabna Revolt 1873-1876 Deccan Revolt 1874-1875

question: Which of the following aspects of the revolt of 1857 is not correct?
options: It had a diverse social participation
It was enthusiastically supported by the educated elite everywhere
It was great symbol of communal unity
It was limited only to northern India
explanation: Starting from Meerut, the revolt of 1857 began to spread in other parts of the country and emerged in its drastic form in modern Uttar Pradesh which was famous with the name of North-West Frontier and Awadh at that time. The revolt did not effect the southern part of the country except a few of this part. The intellectual class did not take part in this revolt. The revolt had neither an organised planning nor a programme, so, it remained unorganised and confined to some particular places. The British government was helped by the rulers of Patiala, Gwalior and Hyderabad in order to supress the revolt. In the absence of the participation of all classes of society, the revolt failed.

The adopted son of Peshwa Baji Rao II

question: What was the main cause of the failure of the revolt of 1857?

Its effect was within limited area
explanation: The major cause of the failure of the revolt of 1857 was lack of common strategy and central organization. The different groups participated in the revolt had their own interest. There was no feeling of nationalism behind the mutiny and lack of clear vision. Some other causes of the failure of the revolt of 1857 were expansion in limited areas, lack of unity and planning, no unified leadership and discipline, return of British troops from Crimea, no support of native rulers, non-cooperation of Sikhs and Punjabis as well as educated Indian middle class, the Scindia of Gwalior, the Holkars of Indore, the Nizam of Hyderabad, the Raja of Jodhpur, the Nawab of Bhopal, the rulers of Patiala, Sindh and Kashmir and the Rana of Nepal provided active support to the British. explanation: Marching of sepoys to Delhi’s red fort was the first event relating to the war of independence of 1857. The war started from Meerut when the sepoys refused to use the new rifle cartridges and revolted openly. They left Meerut and moved to Delhi. General Hewitt had not tried to stop this revolt. However General Vilobi resisted but he was defeated. The mutineers declared Bahadur Shah Zafar as the emperor of whole of India. explanation: Bakht Khan was the Commander-in-Chief of Indian rebel forces in the Indian Rebellion of 1857 against the East India Company. Bakht Khan was a Pashtun related to the family of Rohilla chief Najib- ul-Daula from the Barech tribe. When Bakht Khan heard of the rebellion in Meerut, he decided to march to Delhi to support the Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar's army. By the time Bakht Khan arrived at Delhi on 1 July 1857 with a large number of Rohilla sepoys, the city had already been taken over by rebel forces and the Mughal ruler Bahadur Shah Zafar had been proclaimed Emperor of India. Soon the superior abilities of Bakht Khan became evident and emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar gave him the authority and title of ‘Saheb-e-Alam Bahadur’.

question: Which dynasty supported British maximum during the 1857 Freedom Movement?
explanation: The British got the maximum support from the Scindias of Gwalior, the Nizam of Hyderabad and Holkars of Indore during the freedom struggle of 1857. They helped the British in suppressing the revolt by all possible means. Along with them the landlords, money lenders (Sahukars) and merchants kept them away from the movement as it was against their economic benefits. Many native rulers like the rulers of Patiala, Jind, Hyderabad, Sikh of Punjab and Gwalior helped the British in suppressing the revolt by every possible means. The educated Indian middle class also did not take part in the freedom struggle of 1857. On the contrary they appreciated the feelings of rebels due to national sentiments. question: Which of the following was not a reason for making the sepoys of the East India Company rebellions?
options: The efforts of the officers of the company to spread Christianity
The order to the sepoys to traveled on ships
explanation: The Revolt of 1857, was the result of the sepoys dissatisfaction against the discrimination by the British government and public revolt emerged in the north and central part of India. This revolt abolished the Company Rule and made the way for the Crown to govern on Indian Peninsula for the next 90 years. The use of greased catridges by the sepoys was considered as the main reason for the revolt but it proved only a catalyst in triggering the revolt. In reality, this revolt was the aggregate result of social, economic, political and religious discontents which were simmering for a long time. The British intervention in Indian social, religious affairs like, the eradication of Sati Pratha, Hindu Widow Remarriage Act etc. created a deep discontent among Indians. It led a notion among Indians that the company officials are trying to promote Christianity and their own religions were in grave danger.

question: When was the Criminal Tribes Act enacted for the first time?
explanation: In 1871 AD, the colonial government in India passed the Criminal Tribes Act. By this Act many communities of craftsmen, traders and pastoralists were classified as criminal tribes. They were stated to be criminal by nature and by birth. Once this Act came into force, these communities were expected to live only in notified village settlements. They were not allowed to move out without a permit. The village police kept a continuous watch on them. This Act was first implemented in northern India and later in Bengal and Madras presidency in 1876 AD and 1911 AD respectively.

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Who was the leader of Munda revolt?
explanation: The tribal rebellion against the British also known as Ulgulan rebellion was organized by Birsa Munda also known as 'Dharti Aba' or 'Father of Earth'. He was a tribal, freedom fighter, religious leader and folk hero who belonged to Munda tribe from Chhota Nagpur (Jharkhand)th area. He had led Munda rebellion towards end of 19 century against the British Raj. Anand Pandey was teacher of Birsa Munda. Their movement identified as 'Sardari Ladai' or 'War of the Leaders', was fought with the aim of expelling Dikhus and restoration of the Munda domination over their homeland. The tribal chiefs rose up against the erosion of Khuntkatti system or joint tenures. Starting in 1895 AD, the revolt was against interference by British administration which transformed tribal agrarian system into feudal state around Chhota Nagpur area as well as interference in their religious matters from missionary activities. Birsa Munda had adopted ‘Guerilla Warfare’ techniques to launch surprise attacks in which many police officials were killed. The revolt was brutally suppressed by Britishers. Birsa Munda was arrested and was sentenced to death and died in jail of Cholera. “Aranyer Adhikar” which means “Right to the Forest” was a novel of Mahasweta Devi published in 1977. This novel was based upon the Munda rebellion and Mahasweta Devi got “Sahitya Akademi Award” in 1979 for this work.
source: UPPCS (Pre) G.S. 1998 · Modern India GS p.49

Faced by high prices charged by the British traders for indigo dye, German chemists had already started their search for making synthetic indigo. The synthetic dye was much cheaper and deatt the final blow to the natural plant produced indigo dye. This is the main reason for the decline of indigo cultivation in India by the beginning of 20th century.

options: the reduction of the share of the landlords from one-half of the crop to one-third
the grant of ownership of land to peasants as they were the actual cultivators of the land
the uprooting of Zamindari system and the end of serfdom
explanation: The Tebhaga Movement was a militant campaign initiated in Bengal by the Kisan Sabha in 1946. The demand of the Tebhaga Peasant Movement was for the reduction of share of the landlords from one-half of the crop to one-third. The prominent leaders of the movement were the Kansari Halder, Ganesh Das, Ashok Bose. The movement continued till 1950, when the Bargadari Act was enacted which provided that the share of the harvest given to the landlords would be limited to one third of the total.

The sect was founded by Karam Shah of North Bengal. His son Tipu Shah led these people to uphold the religion and rights of the peasants in Bengal. Tipu captured Sherpur in 1825 AD and assumed royal power. He appointed a judge, a magistrate and a collector to control the administration. The insurgents extended their activities to Garo Hills. The area remained disturbed till the 1830s and 1840s.

explanation: Bijolia was the very first peasant movement of India which started in Bijolia (now in Bhilwara district) of Mewar principality in 1897 AD. The movement took place in three stages. It was a movement against excessive revenue extortion- First Stage- 1897 to 1916 under the leadership of Sadhu Sitaram Das, was marked by spontaneous movement. Second Stage- 1916 to 1923 under the leadership of Vijay Singh Pathik, saw a rise in the consciousness of the peasant class. Third Stage- 1923 to 1941 under the leadership of Manikya Lal Verma, saw a decline in movement.

It was led by the relatively better-off sections of the peasantry, who were called Kunbi peasants in Maharashtra. Which of the statement(s) given above is/ are correct?
explanation: Deccan riots was a peasant revolt but not a movement of the poor tribals or landless peasants. It was led by the relatively better-off sections of the peasantry, who were called Kunbi peasants in Maharashtra. In 1875, the peasants of Maharashtra in some parts of Pune, Satara and Ahmednagar districts revolted against increasing agrarian distress. The Deccan riots of 1875 targeted conditions of debt peonage (Kamiuti) to moneylenders. The rioters specific purpose was to obtain and destroy the bonds, decrees and other documents in the possession of the money lenders. Thus, both statement 1 & 2 are correct.

question: In the context of Indian history, the Rukhmabai case of 1884 revolved around 1. women’s right to gain education 2. age of consent 3. restitution of conjugal rights Select the correct answer using the code given below:
explanation: Rukhmabai, one among the first Indian women to practice medicine in colonial India, made her mark in history due to the legal case she was involved in, which contributed to the enactment of the Age of Consent Act, 1891. She lost her father when she was eight years old and was married off at the age of 11 to Dadaji Bhikaji. Rukhmabai refused to move in with her husband stating that a woman cannot be compelled to stay in a wedlock when she is not interested. The Dadaji Bhikaji vs. Rukhmabai case that went on for three years triggered a debate in both England and India. The verdict went in favour of Dadaji. The court History of Modern India 7 ordered Rukhmabai to live with her husband or face six months imprisonment. A brave Rukhmabai said she was willing to opt the latter. The verdict was subsequently overruled by Queen Victoria. This prompted the government to bring the Age of Consent Act, 1891, despite opposition from conservative Indians.
source: UPSC IAS (Pre) 2020 · Modern India GS p.71

explanation: Raja Ram Mohan Roy founded Brahmo Samaj in Kolkata in 1828. It was a reformist movement within Hinduism. question: Consider the following statements: Assertion (A) : Socio-religious movements of the 19th century resulted in the modernization of India. Reason (R) : Rationalism, scientific temper and other such ideas which are the basis of modernization were at the core of the socio- religious movements. Select the correct answer from the code given below: Codes:
options: Both (A) and (R)are true but (R) is not correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
explanation: The beginning of the Social Reform Movements in India during the 19th century were clearly the outcome of coming in contact of two different societies, totally different from each other. On the one hand, there is the traditional orthodox society and on the other hand is the British educated young generation. There were attempts made by the educated young Indians to end the evils and abuses in religion and society. The western ideas of reason, equality, liberty and humanity inspired them. They tried to remove the defects in their culture. They wanted to revive the glory of Indian culture. Hence we call the socio-religious reform movement of the 19th century India as the Indian Renaissance Movement. Socio-religious movements of the 19th century resulted in the modernization of India. Rationalism, scientific temper and other such ideas which are the basis of modernization were at the core of the socio-religious movements. Hence, both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

question: Which of the following led to the introduction of British Education in India? 1. Charter Act of 1813 2. General Committee of Public Instruction, 1823 3. Orientalist and Anglicist Controversy Select the correct answer using the code given below
explanation: The Charter Act of 1813, incorporated the principle of encouraging learned Indians and promoting knowledge of modern sciences in the country. The Act directed the Company to sanction 1 lakh rupees annually for this purpose. In 1823 AD, the Governor - General -in Council appointed a “General Committee of Public Instruction”, which had the responsibility to grant the 1 lakh of rupees for education. That committee consisted of 10 European members belonging to 2 groups- Anglicists and Orientalists under the Presidentship of Lord Macaulay. Hence, it promoted both Indian and British education. Orentalist-Anglicist Controversy: Within the General Committee on Public Instruction, the Anglicists argued that the government spending on education should be exclusively for modern studies. The Orientalists said while western sciences and literature should be taught to prepare students to take up jobs, emphasis should be placed on expansion of traditional Indian learning. Even the Anglicists were divided over the question of medium of instruction—one faction was for British language as the medium, while the other faction was for Indian languages (vernaculars) for the purpose. Lord Macaulay's Minute (1835), is a famous minute which settled the row in favour of Anglicists—the limited government resources were to be devoted to teaching of western sciences and literature through the medium of British language alone. Hence all the options are correct.
source: IAS (Pre) 2018 · Modern India GS p.92

English was introduced as a medium of higher education on the advice of his (Bentinck) council member, Thomas Babington Macaulay.

question: The propounder of “Filtration Theory” in India’s education policy was-
explanation: During the British rule in India, the downwards filtration theory was adopted in the country. Filtration means coming of something to the bottom from the top. Thus the filtration theory in education meant coming down of education or knowledge from the top to the bottom, i.e., from the higher class people to the middle classes or the general people. The British planned to educate a small section of upper and middle classes Indians thus creating a class "Indian in blood and colour but British in tastes, in opinions, in morals and in intellect who would act as interpreters between the Government and masses and would enrich the vernaculars by which knowledge of western sciences and literature would reach the masses. This was called 'downward filtration theory'. This theory was propounded by Lord Macaulay. He explained his point of view by stating that “the purpose of East India Company was only to educate the elite class which would educate the general public later-thus fulfilling the goal of educating the masses in general.”
source: RAS/RTS (Pre) G.S. 2013 UP Lower (Pre) 2013 · Modern India GS p.92

The recommendation was accepted by William Bentinck and in 1835 AD the Government Resolution made english as the official and literary language of India. english was made as the medium of instruction in schools and colleges which were opened by the British Government.

question: Who among the following repealed the Vernacular Press Act of 1878?
explanation: The Vernacular Press Act was passed by Lord Lytton in 1878 AD. According to this Act, the vernacular or the local newspapers could not print any material or information that could provoke people against the British rule. By this Act, the magistrates of the districts were empowered to such an extent that no appeal would be entertained in court of a law related to vernacular press without the prior permission of the Government, Thus the Vernacular Press Act of 1878 gagged the press and result of some proceedings were against vernacular press people. There was strong opposition to the Act. The Act was later repealed by Lord Ripon in 1881 AD, who followed Lord Lytton.

Sir John Sargent, the Educational Adviser to the Government of India was asked to prepare a comprehensive report on education. For the purpose, the government formed a Committee of Enquiry with 22 members. The report of the committee was submitted to the Central Advisory Board of Education (CABE) in 1944. The Board accepted it and recommended its enforcement. The scheme was known as ‘Sargent Scheme of Education’ as it was prepared by John Sargent. Hunter Education Commission was founded in 1882 by Lord Ripon (1880-1884 AD). The government appointed the commission under the chairmanship of William Wilson Hunter to review the progress made in the field of education by Charles Wood’s declaration in 1854. In 1854 AD the President of the Board of Control of the East India Company sent the “Wood’s despatch” also termed as Magnacarta of British Education in India" to the Governor General Lord Dalhousie. In accordance with Wood’s despatch, Education Departments were established in every province and universities were opened at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras in 1857 on the model of the London University. question: The aim of education as stated by the Wood’s despatch of 1854 was:
options: the creation of employment opportunities for native Indians.
the spread of western culture in India.
the promotion of literacy among the people using British medium of language.
the introduction of scientific research and rationalism in the traditional Indian education.
explanation: In 1854 AD, Charles Wood, the President of Board of Directors prepared a despatch on the educational system for India. Considered the "Magnacarta of British Education in India", this document was the first comprehensive plan for the spread of education in India. The despatch first throws light on the aims and objectives of educational policy of the Company in India. It gave highest priority to the University Education. The Despatch had the following objectives in view: (i) An education department was to be set up in every province. (ii) Universities on the model of the London University to be established in big cities such as Bombay, Calcutta and Madras. (iii) At least one government school to be opened in every district. (iv) Affiliated private schools should be given grant in aid. (v) The Indian natives should be given training in their mother tongue also. (vi) Provision was made for a systematic method of education from primary level to the university level. (vii) It laid stress on female and vocational education and on teachers training.
source: IAS (Pre) G.S. 2003 · Modern India GS p.93

Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
explanation: Allan Octavian Hume was a retired civilian officer who founded Indian National Union in 1884. After his journey to Kolkata, Mumbai and Madras he took the vow to organise the first Indian National Union meet in Pune (early Poona) with the objective to obtain a share in government for educated Indians and to create a platform for civil and political dialogue between educated Indians and British rule. The first session of Indian National Union was held on December 28, 1885 where on the advice of Dadabhai Naoroji the organization was renamed as ‘Indian National Congress’.

explanation: Congress passed the resolution of independence of India for the first time in Madras Session, 1927. This session was presided over by Dr. M. A. Ansari. Pt. Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhash Chandra Bose formed ‘Independence for India League’ in Congress to achieve the target of complete independence.
source: MPPSC (Pre) G.S. 1996 · Modern India GS p.112

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Where did the 27th Session of Indian National Congress take place?
explanation: The 27th Session of Indian National Congress was held between December 26-28, 1912 at Bankipore under the Chairmanship of R. N. Madholkar.
source: BPSC (Pre) 2011 · Modern India GS p.112

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Which Congress President negotiated both Cripps Mission and Lord Wavell?
explanation: Abul Kalam Azad negotiated Cripps Mission in 1942 and Lord Wavell in 1945. He was twice elected President of the Indian National Congress, the first time in 1923 when he was only 35 years old, and the second time in 1940. He continued as the President of the Congress till 1946.
source: BPSC (Pre) 2004-05 · Modern India GS p.112

subject: AP & Indian History
question: In the following industrialists, who was the cashier of A.I.C. for the longest time and also went to jail in 1930?
explanation: Jamnalal Bajaj was an Indian industrialist, a philanthropist, and Indian independence fighter. He was also a close associate and follower of Mahatma Gandhi. At the age of 30 he took part in Indian National Congress. In protest of the British government's policy towards India, he rejected the title of ‘Rai Bahadur'. He was the Cashier in Indian National Congress from 1920 to 1942.
source: BPSC (Pre) 2004-05 · Modern India GS p.112

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Who presided Delhi Session of Indian National Congress in 1947?
options: Jawaharlal Nehru History of Modern India
explanation: The British Government declared Congress an illegal organization during Quit Indian Movement. As a result the Congress leaders were taken captive. No annual session of Congress was held between 1941 to 1945. When Congress Committee accepted the proposal of divided India in Delhi on June 14, 1947, J. B. Kriplani was the Chairman of Indian National Congress. This proposal was presented by Govind Vallabh Pant and supported by Maulana Abul Kalam Azad, Sardar Patel and Jawaharlal Nehru. J. B. Kriplani resigned from Congress chairmanship on November 1, 1947 after which Dr. Rajendra Prasad became interim chairman of Congress. Pattabhi Sitaramyya became the Chairman of Indian National Congress in Jaipur Session in 1948.
source: BPSC (Pre) 2004-05 · Modern India GS p.112

subject: AP & Indian History
question: During the meeting of the Congress Working Committee (April-May 1947) held in Allahabad, one member from the following members was able to mobilize a majority in the favour of Guerrilla warfare against Japan due to his ideology of anti-Nazism, anti-fascism and the anti-imperialist stance. He was-
explanation: Jawaharlal Nehru was one of the very few Asian nationalist leaders who had a clear perception on Nazism, fascism and imperialism and who draw political conclusions from his standpoint. During the meeting of the Congress Working Committee (April- May 1947) held in Allahabad, Jawaharlal Nehru was able to mobilize a majority in the favour of Guerrilla warfare against Japan due to his ideology of Anti- Nazism, anti-fascism and the anti-imperialist stance.
source: BPSC (Pre) 2003-04 · Modern India GS p.112

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Who presided over the second session of Indian National Congress?
explanation: The second session of Indian National Congress under the chairmanship of Dadabhai Naoroji was held at Calcutta in 1886.
source: BPSC (Pre) G.S. 2002 · Modern India GS p.112

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Which of the following session of Indian National Congress was not presided over by Jawaharlal Nehru?
explanation: The 53rd Session of Indian National Congress was held at Ramgarh in 1940 under the Chairmanship of Abul Kalam Azad while Jawaharlal Nehru presided over the Lahore, Lucknow and Faizpur Session of Indian National Congress.
source: UP UDA/LDA Spl. 2006 · Modern India GS p.112

subject: AP & Indian History
question: For how many times Madan Mohan Malviya became the President of Indian National Congress?
explanation: Madan Mohan Malviya presided over 2 sessions of Indian National Congress. Firstly he presided over the Lahore Session (23rd Session) in 1909 followed by Delhi Session (33rd Session) in 1918.
source: UP UDA/LDA Spl. 2006 · Modern India GS p.113

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Who said that 'Congress Movement was neither inspired by the people nor devised or planned by them'?
explanation: Lala Lajpat Rai said at the Congress Session of 1888 at Allahabad, “The Congress movement was neither inspired by the people nor devised or planned by them. It was a movement not from within; the leaders had neither sufficient political consciousness nor faith; they had political opinions but not beliefs.”
source: BPSC (Pre) 2004-05 · Modern India GS p.113

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Who among the following was never associated with Indian National Congress?
explanation: Sir Syyed Ahmad Khan was never associated with Indian National Congress. He founded Anglo- Mohammadan School at Aligarh in 1875 which later became Aligarh Muslim University.
source: Uttarakhand UDA (Pre) 2003 · Modern India GS p.113

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Who was the President of Gaya Session of the Indian National Congress held in 1922?
explanation: Famous by the name of ‘Deshbandhu’ Chittranjan Das was the President of Gaya Session of the Indian National Congress held in 1922. Motilal Nehru along with Chittranjan Das founded Swaraj Party in 1923.
source: BPSC (Pre) 2015 · Modern India GS p.113

subject: AP & Indian History
question: “Swaraj is my birthright, I shall have it” Tilak expressed this statement for the first time in the following session of Indian National Congress-
explanation: Bal Gangadhar Tilak in Lucknow session of Indian National Congress held in 1916 vigorously proclaimed “Swaraj is my birth right, I shall have it.”
source: UPPCS (Pre) G.S. 1998 MPPSC (Pre) G.S. 1990, 93, 95, 98 UPPCS (Mains) Spl. G.S. 2004 Uttarakhand PCS (M) 2006 UPPCS (Mains) Ist G.S. 2015 BPSC (Pre) 1998, 2000-01, 2003-04 · Modern India GS p.113

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Which one among the following explains the meaning of the 'Safety Valve Theory' in the context of Indian National Movement?
options: A theory that argued that the Congress was formed as a safe outlet to the discontented educated Indians
A theory that argued that the Congress was formed as a safe outlet to the hostile attitude of the British towards the Indian people
A theory which believed that the British and the ex-rebels of 1857 should amicably resolve their differences against each other
An idea aimed at promoting goodwill among the Indian people
explanation: The concept of Safety Valve Theory says that the British had seen the political situation in the country leading to another rebellion on the lines of the Mutiny of 1857; and they wished to avoid such a situation. So, they wanted to provide a platform to the people, where they could discuss their political problems. Indian National Congress was founded by a Retired Civil Servant, A. O Hume with the support of 72 political activists on December 28, 1885. A O. Hume and other British thought that the educated Indians may become leaders of the Indian public and organize a rebellion against the government. So if the Government itself provides them a platform to raise their voice, it may be possible to stop such nuisance. 15. Moderat National C
source: UPSC CAPF G.S. Ist 2014 · Modern India GS p.113

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Who called the Congress Conferences as the “Annual National Festival of Educated Indians”?
explanation: The Moderate leaders were accused of limiting the range of their activities for the benefit of the middle-class intelligentsia and limiting the membership of the Congress to the middle class—for fear of losing their leadership if the masses joined the movement. The Moderate leaders were accused of ‘trading in the name of patriotism. Tilak described the Congress as a Congress of flatterers and Congress session ‘a holiday recreation while Lajpat Rai dubbed Congress meeting the annual national festival of educated Indians.’ Both Tilak and Lajpat Rai believed that the Congress had no constructive activity. Tilak affirmed: “We will not achieve any success in our labours if we croak once a year like a frog.”
source: MPPSC Pre 2022 · Modern India GS p.114

subject: AP & Indian History
question: The early leadership of the Indian National Congress was______in its methods and aims.
explanation: The moderates contributed significantly in Indian freedom struggle. The main objective of the moderates was to achieve self government within the British Empire. They followed a middle path and not an extreme path against British Empire. The 1885-1905 phase of Indian National Congress was dominated by moderates.
source: Mizoram PSC-2021 · Modern India GS p.114

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Which of the following stressed on giving self- government to India continuously since 1904?
explanation: Swaraj (self-rule) was articulated in the presidential address of Dadabhai Naoroji as the goal of Congress in its Calcutta Session held in 1906. Although the word ‘Swaraj was first used by Swami Dayanand Saraswati. History of Modern India 12 te Period of Indian Congress 1885-1905
source: UPPCS (Mains) G.S. Ist 2016 · Modern India GS p.114

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Who amongst the following continuously emphasised on giving self-rule to India in 1904, 1905 and 1906?
explanation: Bal Gangadhar Tilak was a leader of the Indian Independence movement. He continuously emphasized self-rule for India and spearheaded the Swadeshi Movement during 1904-1906 as the leader of the extremist faction. He was called as the 'Father of Indian Unrest’ by Valentine Chirol. • He is also known as Lokmanya Tilak and he is the founder of the Deccan Education Society (1884) along with his associate Gopal Ganesh Agarkar and others.
source: OPSC (OCS)-2018 Paper-I · Modern India GS p.114

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Swaraj was first placed as a national demand by-
explanation: In 1906, the Congress Session at Calcutta was presided over by Dadabhai Naoroji. The moderates chose Dadabhai Naoroji to preside the Congress. Dadabhai Naoroji, the ‘Grand Oldman’ of India was respected by the moderates and extremists alike. But, in this session, the Congress was compelled by the extremists to adopt following resolutions which were accepted by the moderates with half heart. These were as follows- (i) Resolution on National Education (ii) Resolution of Self Rule (Swaraj) (iii) Resolution on Swadeshi (iv) Resolution on Boycott. Thus Swaraj was first placed as a national demand in Calcutta session of 1906.
source: Uttarakhand PCS (Pre) 2002-03 · Modern India GS p.114

explanation: Dadabhai Naoroji who presided over the second session of the Congress at Calcutta in 1886 AD made the statement “Kings are made for Public; Public is not made for King.” He was the first Indian elected to the British House of Commons. He contested on the ticket of Liberal Party in 1892 AD. History of Modern India

He worked as a professor of Gujarati in the University College, London.
He laid the foundation of woman’s education in Bombay.
He was elected as a member of British Parliament on the ticket of Conservative Party.

question: Which one of the following statements is not correct about Dadabhai Naoroji?
options: He was the first Indian to be appointed as professor of Mathematics and Physics at Elphinstone College, Bombay.
He was elected as the member of British Parliament in 1892.
He started a Gujarati Journal, 'Rast Goftar'.
For four times he had presided over the Indian National Congress.
explanation: Dadabhai Naoroji was the first Indian to be appointed as professor of Mathematics and Physics at Elphinstone College, Bombay. He was elected as the member of British Parliament in 1892 AD. He started a Gujarati Journal, 'Rast Goftar'. He presided over only three sessions of Indian National Congress, Calcutta Session in 1886, Lahore Session in 1893 and 22nd Session at Calcutta in 1906. Hence statement (d) is incorrect.

subject: AP & Indian History
question: A committee was constituted in 1889 to get support for Congress. Who among the following was the president of that committee?
explanation: The official organ of Indian National Congress in London was known as the British Committee of Indian National Congress. The British Committee of the Congress was formed on July 27, 1889 with Sir W. Wedderburn as its chairman and William Digby as its secretary. Its purpose was to raise awareness of Indian issues among the public in Britain.
source: RAS/RTS (Pre) G.S. 1996 · Modern India GS p.116

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Which of the following nationalist leaders has been described as extremist in politics and conservative in social subjects?
explanation: Balgangadhar Tilak has been described as extremist in politics and conservative in social subjects. He opposed ‘Age of Consent’ bill as he believed that foreigners have no right to make laws for our society. His ideology was that society could be reformed by educating the people.
source: Uttarakhand PCS (M) 2004-05 · Modern India GS p.116

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Who among the following was not a moderate?
explanation: Surat split 1907 refers to the split of Congress party in two groups: Moderates and Extremist. Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Bipin Chandra Pal and Aurobindo Ghosh were related to extremist group of Indian National Congress. While the moderates include the leaders like Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Madan Mohan Malviya, Dadabhai Naoroji, S. N. Banerjee, Firoz Shah Mehta and Badruddin Tyabji.
source: UPPCS (Pre) G.S. 1995 · Modern India GS p.116

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Who accused Indian national congress of practicing ‘politics of prayer, petition and protest’?
explanation: Bal Gangadhar Tilak accused Indian National Congress of practicing the politics of prayer, petition and protest. He said “Three P's-pray, pleas and protest- will not do unless backed by solid force.” History of Modern India
source: UPPCS (Pre) G.S. 2001 UP Lower (Pre) Spl. 2002 · Modern India GS p.116

question: Who called Indian National Congress a 'begging institute'?
explanation: In 1893-94, Aurobindo Ghosh published an article series called 'New Lamps for Old' in Indu Prakash in which he made the first systematic criticism of liberal politics. In his criticism he called the Congress a ‘begging institute.’
source: UP Lower (Pre) Spl. 2008 · Modern India GS p.116

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Who propounded the theory of passive resistance?
explanation: The concept of passive resistance was highlighted by Aurobindo Ghosh. He was against the Moderates’ theory of “politics of petition” and along with Tilak belonged to the extremist section of Indian National Congress. In place of prayer, petition, protest and “pleas”, he advocated the more radical policy of boycott. He visualized that other nations had won the precious prize of liberty by ‘intense suffering, humiliations and martyrdom’, than ‘merely by spending the ink of the journalist and petition-framer and the breath of the orator’. In view of Aurobindo, the politics of petitioning was “the dream of timid inexperience, the teaching of false friends who hope to keep us in perpetual subjection, foolish to reason, false to experience“. In view of Aurobindo Ghosh, the Moderates displayed only sentimental enthusiasm.
source: BPSC (Pre) 2004-05 · Modern India GS p.116

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Assertion (A): The basic weakness of the early nationalist movement lay in its narrow social base. Reason (R): It fought for the narrow interests of the social groups which joined it. Code:
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The basic weakness of the early nationalist movement lay in its narrow social base because in the early stages moderate leadership (Dadabhai Naoroji, Mahadev Govind Ranade, Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Feroz Shah Mehta, Surendra Nath Banerjee etc.) was at its peak. But this liberal leadership did not fight for narrow interests of social groups instead they wanted to raise consciousness in the uneducated public. Later, they became the founder of India's extensive public awareness and social movement. The impact of their ideas was the basis of the upcoming political background. Thus the assertion (A) of the question is true, but the reason (R) is false.
source: IAS (Pre) G.S. 2000 · Modern India GS p.116

question: Consider the following statements: Assertion (A): Bal Gangadhar Tilak was a communalist. Reason: He used religion as a political weapon. Choose the correct option from the code given below- Code:
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A

explanation: Bal Gangadhar Tilak was an extremist national leader not communalist. Hence the assertion (A) is incorrect. He started Ganapati festival in 1893. By doing so, he transformed the traditional Ganapati festival of Maharashtra into a National festival. He also started Shivaji Mahotsava in Maharashtra in 1895. The purpose of celebrating these festivals was linked to self- pride and national unity. Bal Gangadhar Tilak, the nationalist and 'the father of Indian unrest' as described by the British was the man behind turning a private household Ganesh Chaturthi celebration to a gala event. Hence we can say that he had used religion as a political weapon.
source: UPPCS (Pre) G.S. 2001 · Modern India GS p.117

question: A graduate at 18, professor and associate editor of the Sudharak at 20, Secretary of the Sarvajanik Sabha and of the Provincial Conference at 25, Secretary of the National Congress at 29, leading witness before an important Royal Commission at 31, Provincial legislator at 34, Imperial legislator at 36, President of the Indian National Congress at 39 a patriot whom Mahatma Gandhi himself regarded as his master. This is how a biographer describes- History of Modern India
explanation: One of the leaders of the moderate bloc of the Indian National Congress and Mahatma Gandhi’s political mentor, Gopal Krishna Gokhale was born on May 9, 1866 at Kotluk in district Ratnagiri in modern- day Maharashtra to Krishna Rao Gokhale and his wife Valubai. He secured his graduate degree at the age of 18 years from Bombay’s Elphinstone College in the year 1884. He worked in Pune as a school teacher. He later taught economics and history at Fergusson College at the age of 20 years. In 1905, Gokhale established the Servants of India Society for expanding education among Indians. In 1889, Gokhale joined the INC motivated by his mentor and social reformer M. G. Ranade. At the age of 39 he presided over Banaras Session of Indian National Congress held in 1905.

subject: AP & Indian History
question: The method of moderate leaders of Congress was-
explanation: The main objective of the moderates was to achieve self-government within the British empire. In order to achieve this aim they made several demands for reforms and indulged in criticizing the government policies. They believed in patience and reconciliation rather than in violence and confrontation. They relied on constitutional and peaceful methods in order to achieve their aim. The moderates believed in orderly progress and constitutional agitation. They believed in constitutional agitation within the four corners of law and also they believed that their main task was to educate the people, to arouse national political consciousness and to create a united public opinion on political questions
source: BPSC (Pre) 2007-08 · Modern India GS p.117

They advocated boycott of foreign goods

They comprehended the vital role played by India in the imperial economy of Britain
explanation: The moderate leaders like Mahadev Govind Ranade, Dadabhai Naoroji, W.C. Banerjee, Gopal Krishna Gokhale and Firoz Shah Mehta etc. criticized the British for drain of wealth from India. They advocated boycott of foreign goods. They ignored the issue of exploitation of Indian rural people by the zamindars. Option (d) is incorrect because they criticized the British for drain of wealth from India.

explanation: Gopal Krishna Gokhale was elected to the Mumbai Legislative Council in 1899 and to the Imperial Legislative Council in 1902. The conflict of Gokhale’s moderate views with the more militant ideas of Bal Gangadhar Tilak led to a breach in the Indian National Congress that nearly immobilized it from 1907 to 1916. In 1905, Gopal Krishna Gokhale had established the Servants of India Society. In the course of the Indian freedom struggle, he rejected the title of ‘Knighthood’ and refused to accept a position in the Council of the Secretary of State in India.

subject: AP & Indian History

question: What was the purpose with which Sir William Wedderburn and W. S. Caine had set up the Indian Parliamentary Committee in 1893?
options: To agitate for Indian political reforms in the House of Commons
To campaign for the entry of Indians into the Imperial Judiciary
To facilitate a discussion on India’s Independence in the British Parliament
To agitate for the entry of eminent Indians into the British Parliament
explanation: To agitate for India's political reforms in the House of Commons, Sir William Wedderburn and W.S. Caine had set up the Indian Parliamentary Committee in 1893. Sir William Wedderburn entered Parliament in 1893 as a Liberal member and sought to voice India's grievances in the House. He was a member of the Royal Commission on Indian Expenditure in 1895. He came to India in 1904 to attend the 20th session of the Indian National Congress in Bombay.

question: With reference to the Civil Administration in 1905, which of the statements is/are correct? 1 . Lord Curzon decided to rearrange the provincial boundaries 2 . A new province was constituted, called East Bengal and Assam Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
explanation: In order to weaken the nationalism among Indians, Lord Curzon decided to rearrange the provincial boundaries. The Partition of Bengal was declared on July 19, 1905 by then Viceroy of India, Lord Curzon (1899-1905) and came into effect on October 16, 1905. The partition took place into two provinces-one province was Eastern Bengal and Assam, with its capital at Dacca. The other province was West Bengal, with its capital Calcutta. As a reaction to the Partition of Bengal, Swadeshi Movement was formally declared on August 7, 1905. in a meeting held at the Calcutta Town Hall. The famous boycott Resolution was passed in this meeting. Tilak called this movement Bahishkar Yoga. S.N. Banerjee said that it is a protectionist movement and later on December 12, 1911 King George V abolished the division of Bengal in a durbar organized at Delhi.
source: UPPCS (Pre) 2019 · Modern India GS p.120

explanation: When Curzon (1899-1905) then Viceroy of India, announced the partition of Bengal in July, 1905, Indian National Congress, initiated Swadeshi Movement in Bengal. Swadeshi Movement was launched as a protest movement which also gave a lead to the Boycott movement in the country. The ‘Swadeshi’ and ‘Boycott’ were adopted as methods of struggle for the first time during the agitation against the Partition of Bengal. Swadeshi movement was officially proclaimed on August 7, 1905 at the Calcutta Town Hall, in Bengal. The movements included using goods produced in India and burning British-made goods. Bal Gangadhar Tilak encouraged Swadeshi and Boycott movement after the British government decided the partition of Bengal. In 1909, the movement had spread across the country and people had started anti- partition and anti-colonial movements.

explanation: Regarding ‘Swadeshi Movement’ statement (d) is incorrect because some specific Muslims were joined in the Swadeshi Movement whereas women’s actively participated in this movement. It was for the first time women took part in any movement. They came outside from their houses, sat to protest and demonstrated in the rallies. This movement affected only high and middle class people but did not influence the farmers of Bengal. Barisal was an exception of it. The movement was not spread only in the region of Bengal. Sir Syed Haider Raza popularised the Swadeshi Movement in Delhi. Chidambaram Pillai spread the movement to Madras and organized the strike of the Tuticorin Coral Mill. Bipin Chandra Pal played a major role in popularizing the movement; especially in the urban areas. Liaqat Hussain took the movement to Patna and organized the East Indian Railway strike in 1906. He also wrote fiery articles in Urdu to rouse nationalist sentiments in Muslims. He was supported by other Muslim Swadeshi agitators like Ghaznavi, Rasul, Din Mohammed, Dedar Bux, Monir-uz-Zaman, Ismail Hussain, Siraji, Abdul Hussain and Abdul Gaffar. Lala Lajpat Rai took the movement to Punjab and of northern India. History of Modern India

question: What was the main reason for the split in the Indian National Congress at Surat in 1907?
options: Introduction of communalism into Indian politics by Lord Minto
Extremists lack of faith in the capacity of the moderates to negotiate with the British Government
Aurobindo Ghosh’s inability to be elected as the President of the Indian National Congress History of Modern India
explanation: Surat Split refers to the splitting of the Indian National Congress into ‘moderates’ and ‘extremists’ after a violent clash at the Surat session of INC held in 1907. Ras Bihari Bose was the President of Surat Session (1907) of INC. The extremists were led by Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Lala Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal and Aurobindo Ghosh and the moderates were led by Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Feroz Shah Mehta and Surendra Nath Banerjee. Moderates believed in the policy of settlement of minor issues with the government by deliberations. But the extremists believed in agitation, strikes and boycotts to force their demands. Some nationalists led by Bal Gangadhar Tilak agitated against the moderate behaviour of congress against British rule. The Moderates did not realise that the council reforms were meant by the government more to isolate the Extremists than to reward the Moderates. The Extremists did not realize that the Moderates could act as their outer line of defense in face of state repression. Both sides did not realise that in a vast country like India ruled by a powerful imperialist country, only a broad-based nationalist movement could succeed. As a result, breakup took place. The divided Congress re-united in the crucial Lucknow session of Indian National Congress in 1916.
source: IAS (Pre) G.S. 2016 · Modern India GS p.126

explanation: The younger brother of Aurobindo Ghosh, Barindra Kumar Ghosh was extremely influenced by his brother hence he joined the revolutionary movement. In 1905 he authored an article in the book ‘Bhawani Mandir’ about the detailed description for the formation of center for organizing revolutionary works and is credited for spreading revolutionary ideas in Bengal along with Bhupendra Nath Dutta. Their activities led to the formation of Anushilan Samiti. The Anushilan Samiti in Calcutta was established by Pramath Nath Mitra, a barrister from Calcutta in 1902. The people associated with this Samiti were Sri Aurobindo, Deshabandhu Chittaranjan Das, Surendranath Tagore, Jatindranath Banerjee, Bagha Jatin, Bhupendra Nath Dutta, Barindra Ghosh etc. The revolutionaries formed many secret organizations in which the most important and long-lasting organizations were Anushilan Samiti, Jugarat, Swadesh Bind Samiti and Vrati Samiti. Their activities were mainly of two types- to kill the tyrannical British officers, informers and anti- nationalists and collect money to buy weapons by dacoity. It was later known as Swadeshi dacoity. Dhaka Anushilan Samiti was a branch of Anushilan Samiti founded in 1902 in Dhaka by Barindra Kumar Ghosh, Satish Chandra Bose and Pulin Bihari Das. Barrah dacoity of June, 1908 was the first major event of Anushilan Samiti. The plan of dacoity was made by Pulin Bihari Bose.

question: Who defended Aurobindo Ghosh in Alipore Bomb Case?
explanation: When Bengal was partitioned it sparked an outburst of public anger against the British. The anger led to civil unrest and a nationalist campaign was carried out by groups of revolutionaries, led by Aurobindo Ghosh, Ras Bihari Bose and Bagha Jatin and organized into groups like Yugantar. The British cracked down hard on the activists and the conflict came to a peak on April 30, 1908 when Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki attempted to kill Magistrate Kingsford. Aurobindo Ghosh was also arrested on charges of planning and overseeing the attack and imprisoned in solitary confinement in Alipore Jail. The trial continued for a year (1908 - 1909), and Ras Bihari Bose was found guilty and later hanged. explanation: Madan Lal Dhingra was a great revolutionary from Punjab associated with the Indian Home Rule Society, Abhinav Bharat Society and the Indian House in London. explanation: On December 30, 1906, around 3000 delegates of which 56 were temporary members attended a conference of the Muhammadan Educational Conference at Dhaka in which the ban on politics was removed and a motion was moved to form the All India Muslim League (AIML). The name was proposed by Nawab Khawaja Sir Salimullah Bahadur and seconded by Hakim Ajmal Khan. The founding meeting was hosted by Nawab Khwaja Salimullah. The AIML was the first Muslim political party of India. Lucknow was the headquarter of All India Muslim League. Nawab Mohasin-ul-Mulk and Nawab Waqar-ul-Mulk were jointly appointed as the Secretary of the Muhammadan Educational Conference. Nawab Waqar-ul-Mulk Mushtaq Hussain was the first president of Muslim League.

Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Deliverance Day was Muslim League's observance of December 22, 1939 as mark of relief on the resignation of all provincial Congress Ministries of British India. They resigned in mass protesting the Viceroy's decision to make India a party to the Second World War without duly consulting Indians. The Congress criticised this move of the league and Mahatma Gandhi appealed to Jinnah to desist from observing this day. The Day of Deliverance was celebrated in many parts of India by Muslim League supporters, as well as some non-Muslim Congress opponents. The latter included the All- India Depressed Classes Association, Dalit leader B.R. Ambedkar and the Independent Labour Party leaders E.V. Ramasamy of the justice party as well as some Parsis, and Anglo- Indians. Hence, both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.

explanation: On March 28, 1929 the Muslim League session was held at Delhi under the presidency of Mohammad Ali Jinnah. In his address to his delegates, he consolidated Muslim viewpoints under fourteen points and these fourteen points became Jinnah's 14 points. The Fourteen Points were proposed by Muhammad Ali Jinnah as a constitutional reform plan to safeguard the political rights of Muslims in a self-governing India. Jinnah produced his fourteen points in response to the Nehru Report in 1929. Jinnah wanted separate Muslim electorates in the British Indian Government, So that the Muslims could have representation of 1/3 in every decision made by the Government of India. The Nehru report said that, there should be joint electorates which were automatically declared as against the Muslims of India and hence they opposed it. That is why Jinnah produced his fourteen points.

He studied at Bombay University and at Lincoln's Inn in London. He then ran a successful legal practice in Bombay. He was already a member of the Indian National Congress, which was working for autonomy from British rule, when he joined the Muslim League in 1913. In 1909, he was elected as Muslim representative from Bombay in the Imperialist Legislative Council. In 1914, he went to London as the representative of Indian National Congress. So we can say that the role of Jinnah from 1906 to 1920 during freedom struggle of India was nationalist and secular.

question: In which province Muslim League formed government after 1946 election?
explanation: Muslim League formed government in Bengal under Fazlul Haq with an alliance of Krishak Praja Party in the elections of 1946. By the December 1946, the elections to the Constituent assembly had taken place. On 6 December 1946, the constituent assembly met for the first time. The members of the constituent assembly were elected by the provincial assemblies by method of single transferable vote system of proportional representations. Total membership of the constituent assembly was 389, out of which 292 were the representatives of the states, 93 were representatives of princely states and 4 were from the Chief Commissioners provinces of Delhi, Ajmer-Mewar, Coorg and British Baluchistan. The elections for the 296 seats assigned to the British Indian provinces were completed by July-August 1946. Congress won 208 seats and Muslim league won 73 seats. The leader of Muslim League in Bengal and Chief Minister of the province was Hussain Suhrawardy.
source: RAS/RTS (Pre) G.S. 2008 · Modern India GS p.145

Besant’s League was set up in September 1916 in Madras and covered the rest of India (including Bombay city). It had 200 branches, was loosely organized as compared to Tilak’s League and had George Arundale as the organizing secretary. The League campaign aimed to convey to the common man the message of Home Rule as self-government. The aim was to be achieved by promoting political education and discussion through public meetings, organizing libraries and reading rooms containing books on national politics, holding conferences, organizing classes for students on politics, propaganda through newspapers, pamphlets, posters, illustrated post-cards, plays, religious songs, etc., collecting funds, organizing social work, and participating in local government activities.

question: When did Mahatma Gandhi established the Sabarmati Ashram in Ahmedabad?
explanation: On his return from South Africa, Gandhi’s first Ashram in India was established in the Kochrab area of Ahmedabad on 25 May 1915. The Ashram was then shifted on 17 June 1917 to a piece of open land on the banks of the river Sabarmati. Reasons for this shift included: he wanted to do some experiments in living e.g, farming, animal husbandry, cow breeding, Khadi and related constructive activities, for which he was in search of this kind of barren land. The Sabarmati Ashram (also known as Harijan Ashram) was home to Mohandas Gandhi from 1917 until 1930 and served as one of the main centres of the Indian freedom struggle. Originally called the Satyagraha Ashram, reflecting the movement toward passive resistance launched by the Mahatma, the Ashram became home to the ideology that set India free.

In Lord Chelmsford's 'War conference', Mahatma Gandhi did not support the resolution on recruiting Indians for world War 3. Consequent upon the breaking of Salt Law by Indian people, the Indian National Congress was declared illegal by the colonial rulers Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: Mahatma Gandhi was instrumental in the abolition of the system of indentured labour. Consequent upon the breaking of Salt Law by Indian people, the Indian National Congress was declared illegal by the colonial rulers. question: What was the reason for Mahatma Gandhi to organize a Satyagraha on behalf of the peasants of Kheda? 1. The administration did not suspend the land revenue collection in spite of a drought. 2. The administration proposed to introduce permanent settlement in Gujarat. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: In Kheda, Gujarat, the peasants were frequently plagued by poverty, famines, scant resource, untouchability, alcoholism and British discrimination. The famine of ‘Chhappania Akal’ and some subsequent famines had destroyed the agrarian economy of the region and the peasants were still dying out of starvation. The Bombay Presidency increased the taxes in 1917-18 by 23%. In 1918, Gujarat as a whole History of Modern India 16 suffered a severe epidemic of Plague and in Kheda alone around 17000 people lost their lives. Further, cholera also broke out locally. The government said that if the taxes are not paid, the property would be seized. This condition of peasants of Kheda provided ample reason for Gandhi to organize the Satyagraha on behalf of them. It was the third Satyagraha movement after Champaran Satyagraha and Ahmedabad mill strike.
source: IAS (Pre) G.S. Ist 2011 · Modern India GS p.161

question: Indian National Congress opposed the Rowlatt Act because it aimed-
options: to ban on Indian National Congress
to imprison national leaders charging the traitors to the nation
explanation: A sedition committee was appointed by the British government during the Viceroyalty of Lord Chelmsford in 1917 with Justice Rowlatt, which made several recommendations to curb sedition activity in India. The Anarchical and Revolutionary Crime Act (1919) popularly known as Rowlatt Act was passed by the Imperial Legislative Council of British India in March, 1919. The Act provided the authority to the British government to arrest and imprison suspects without trial. So like most of the Indians, Indian National Congress disliked this Act because it aimed to limit the individual liberty. In protest to this Act, Swami Shraddhananda suggested starting the movement of not paying rent (Lagaan).

question: In which of the following movements did Mahatma Gandhi make the first use of hunger strike as a weapon?
explanation: Mahatma Gandhi had used hunger strike as a weapon for the first time in Ahmedabad Mill Strike in 1918. In February March 1918, there was a situation of conflict between the Gujarat Mill owners and workers on the question of Plague Bonus of 1917. The Mill Owners wanted to withdraw the bonus but the workers demanded a 50% wage hike. The Mill Owners were willing to give only 20% wage hike. In March 1918, under the leadership of Gandhi, there was a strike in the cotton mills. In this strike Gandhi used the weapon of Hunger strike. The result was that the strike was successful and the workers got a 35% wage increase.

question: Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and other labelled as Reason (R). A is false but R is true

Moulana Mohamed Ali and Abul Kalam Azad resigned from the legislative council in 1919 during Khilafat Movement and not in 1916. In protest against the passing of Rowlatt Act M.A. Jinnah and Madan Mohan Malaviya resigned from the imperial legislative council. 103.Mahatma Gandhi said that some of his deepest convictions were reflected in a book titled, “Unto The Last’’ and the book transformed his life. What was the message from the book that transformed Mahatma Gandhi? History of Modern India 17 (a) Uplifting the oppressed and poor is the moral responsibility of an educated man (b) The good of individual is contained in the good of all (c) The life of celibacy and spiritual pursuit are essential for a noble life (d) All the statements (a), (b) and (c) are correct in this context IAS (Pre) G.S. 2011 Ans-(b) During his stay in South Africa, Mahatma Gandhi read the book ‘Unto The Last’ written by John Ruskin. He later mentioned is his autobiography ‘My Experiment with Truth’ that the book had totally transformed his life. The book consist of the message “The good of the individual is contained in the good of all.”
