question: Karamchand Gandhi was Diwan of-
explanation: Father of Mahatma Gandhi, Karamchand Uttamchand Gandhi (1822–1885) also known as Kaba Gandhi, was a political figure in Porbandar. He served as Diwan of Porbandar, Rajkot, and Bikaner.
source: UPPCS (Pre) G.S. 2001 · Modern India GS p.168

subject: AP & Indian History
question: According to Gandhiji non-violence is-
options: a way to win political freedom
explanation: Satya (Truth) and Ahimsa (Non-Violence) were the two weapons of Mahatma Gandhi during freedom struggle. He considered that truth is achievable and non- violence is a mean to achieve it. Like this according to Mahatma Gandhi non-violence is a way to attain truth. As per the Gandhian philosophy Truth stands for reality. He said “Ahimsa or non-violence is the means and truth is the end. It is impossible to separate them.”
source: UPPCS (Pre) G.S. 1994 · Modern India GS p.168

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Who amongst the following coined the word ‘Satyagraha’?
explanation: After returning from South Africa, Mahatma Gandhi organised a competition for the selection of the term that describes the political struggle in India. The nephew of Mahatma Gandhi, Magan Lal Gandhi first used the term ‘Sada Graha’ for which he was rewarded too. Making a bit of change in the word ‘Sada Graha’, Mahatma Gandhi accepted the word ‘Satyagraha’. Champaran Satyagraha, Bihar of 1917 was the first successful Satyagraha of Mahatma Gandhi.
source: UPPCS (Mains) G.S. Ist 2015 · Modern India GS p.169

subject: AP & Indian History
question: In which of the following railway stations of South Africa, Mahatma Gandhi was thrown out of the train?
explanation: To serve as the legal counsel to the merchant Dada Abdulla, Mahatma Gandhi arrived in South Africa in 1893. Dada Abdulla asked him to undertake a trip from Pretoria in the Transvaal to Pietermaritzburg. There he was seated in the first class compartment as he had purchased a first class ticket. A European entered the compartment hastened to summon railway officials, who ordered Gandhi to shift himself in van compartment. Gandhi protested and showed his ticket; still he along with his luggage was thrown out of the train at the Pietermaritzburg railway station in South Africa on June 7, 1893.
source: UPPCS (Mains) G.S. Ist Paper 2015 · Modern India GS p.169

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Who used the word ‘Sarvodaya’ first?
explanation: Sarvodaya is a term meaning 'Universal Uplift' or 'Progress of All'. The term was first coined by Mohandas Gandhi as the title of his 1908 translation of John Ruskin's abstract on political economy, "Unto This Last", and Gandhi came to use the term for the ideal of his own political philosophy. Later Gandhian, like the Indian nonviolence activist Vinoba Bhave, embraced the term as a name for the social movement in post- independence India.
source: BPSC (Pre) 2003-04 · Modern India GS p.170

subject: AP & Indian History
question: The close compatriot of Mahatma Gandhi during the freedom movement was-
explanation: Charles Andrews also called Deenbandhu Andrews was a professor in St. Stephan’s College, Delhi. He was the close compatriot of Mahatma Gandhi during freedom struggle. Also he was very close to Rabindranath Tagore and Gopal Krishna Gokhale. He accompanied Gandhi as an associate in Round Table Conference in London. He lived with Mahatma Gandhi in Phoenix Farm. Andrews became the president of All India Trade Union in 1925 and served the post till 1927.
source: BPSC (Pre) 2003-04 · Modern India GS p.170

explanation: Mahatma Gandhi did not directly participate in Vaikom Satyagraha. Vaikom Satyagraha was a movement in Travancore (modern-day Kerala) for temple entry of the depressed classes. It took place near the Shiva Temple at Vaikom, Kottayam district, Kerala during 1924-25. Vaikom was at that time a part of the princely state of Travancore.

However, he eventually served only two years of that term. He named Yeravada jail as ‘Mandir’. He wrote ‘Yeravada Mandir’ (Ashram Observance) first published in 1932, translated from Gujarati by Valji Govind Desai.

explanation: Mahatma Gandhi during his stay in South Africa had provided his services as an attendant to the helpless poor patients in the charity hospital of Rustamji. He also served there to the wounded soldiers of the Boer War.

explanation: Mahatma Gandhi was an amalgamation of numerous ideologies, many in one and one in many. Gandhi's socialism was based on high standards. He completely disagreed with Karl Marx's communist policies.

question: According to M. K. Gandhi socio-economic improvement of untouchables can be brought about-

By establishing cottage industry for them
explanation: Mahatma Gandhi mainly stressed on the growth of rural industries such as khadi, handlooms, sericulture, handicrafts etc. He strongly advocated the development of cottage industries as he thought it will reduce the burden from the agricultural sector. He considered that by establishing cottage industries the socio-economic condition of the untouchables could be improved.
source: UP Lower (Mains) 2013 · Modern India GS p.172

question: Which of the following is not a feature of politics of the Gandhian model?
explanation: The exemplification of politics presented by Mahatma Gandhi was the combination of three elements- morality, religion and humanity but there was no place for authority. History of Modern India
source: UP Lower (Mains) 2013 · Modern India GS p.172

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Which of the following statements is not true as per Gandhian Principle?
options: The aim of Satyagrahi is to defeat the enemy
The weapon of Satyagraha is Ahimsa
Satyagrahi should be firm in his belief
Satyagrahi should have no ill feeling towards his enemies
explanation: According to Gandhi’s theory, the objective of the Satyagrahi was not to defeat the enemy but to urge to reveal his truth and to change his heart. Gandhian Satyagraha should be squarely located within conflict resolution discourse. In this principle of non-violence, Mahatma Gandhi introduced technique of resistance to evil and untruth. His Satyagraha is inspired by boundless love and compassion. It is opposed to sin, not sinner, the evil, not evildoer. For him truth was God. Truth is not yours or mine. It is neither Western nor Eastern.
source: UP Lower (Mains) 2013 · Modern India GS p.172

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Whose work have influenced Gandhian concept?
explanation: The Gandhian concept was mainly influenced by the secular writers like Ruskin, Thoreau and Tolstoy etc. The essay based on Civil Disobedience written by Hennery David Thoreau extensively influenced Gandhi. Non-Violence implies bread-labour, which Gandhi derived from Ruskin and Tolstoy and ultimately from the Bible. Gandhi defined it as the ‘Divine Law that man must earn his bread by labouring with his own hands.’ He opted the thought of ‘Sarvodaya’ from Ruskin’s ‘Unto This Last’ and named the book ‘Sarvodaya’ after translating it in Gujarati language. The non-fiction ‘The Kingdom of God is Within You’ by Leo Tolstoy was the base of Non-Cooperation Movement of Mahatma Gandhi.
source: UP Lower (Mains) 2013 · Modern India GS p.172

subject: AP & Indian History
question: As per Mahatma Gandhi politics meant-

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Mahatma Gandhi's severe criticism of the Congress leadership at the opening of the Banaras Hindu University was focused on-
options: the Congress strategy for opposing the government
the Congress accepting offices under the government
condemnation of Indian nationalism for being an elite phenomenon
explanation: Mahatma Gandhi’s first major public appearance was at the opening of the Banaras Hindu University (BHU) in February 1916. When his turn came to speak, Gandhi charged the Indian elite with a lack of concern for the labouring poor. At the opening of the BHU, he said, “certainly a most gorgeous show”. But he worried about the contrast between the “richly bedecked noblemen” present and “millions of the poor” Indians who were absent. It is worth notable that Banaras Hindu University was founded by Pt. Madan Mohan Malviya in 1916 on the occasion of Basant Panchami.
source: UPSC CAPF G.S. Ist 2013 · Modern India GS p.173

Mirajkar, Shaukat Usmani, Philip Spratt etc. were arrested on the charge of conspiracy to overthrow the British Government of India through strikes and other militant methods. It is interesting to note that the accused in the Meerut Case gained the sympathy of the nationalists. options: A political party based in Taiwan
A naval ship of voyage to Canada
A Chinese village where Mao Tse Tung began his long march
explanation: The Komagatamaru was a Japanese steamship chartered by an affluent Punjabi businessman, Gurdip Singh to bring Indian immigrants to Canada. The Ship sailed from British Hong Kong, via Shanghai, China, and Yokohama, Japan, to Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada, in 1914, carrying 376 passengers from Punjab, British India. Of them, 24 were admitted to Canada, but the other 352 passengers were not allowed to disembark in Canada. When the steamship reached Budge-Budge port at Calcutta, the police went to arrest Baba Gurdip Singh and the twenty or so other men that they viewed as leaders. He resisted arrest, a friend of his assaulted a policeman and a general riot ensued. Shots were fired and 18 of the passengers were killed and 202 passengers were sent to jail.

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Who was the founder of Swaraj Party?
explanation: After the Chauri-Chaura incident, Mahatma Gandhi withdrew the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1922. This was met with a lot of disagreements among leaders of the Congress Party. While some wanted to continue Non-Cooperation Movement, others wanted to end the legislature boycott and contest elections. They formally were called no-changers and such leaders included Rajendra Prasad, Sardar Vallabhai Patel, C. Rajagopalachari, etc. The others who wanted to enter the legislative council and obstruct the British government from within were called the pro-changers. These leaders included C. R. Das, Motilal Nehru, Srinivasa Iyengar, etc. In 1922, in the Gaya session of the Congress, C. R. Das (who was presiding over the session) moved a proposal to enter the legislatures but it was defeated. In January, 1923 C. R. Das and other leaders broke away from the Congress and formed the Swaraj Party or the Congress-Khilafat Swaraj Party. C. R. Das was the President and the Secretary was Motilal Nehru. Prominent leaders of the Swaraj Party included N. C. Kelkar, Hussain Shaheed Suhrawardy, Vitthal Bhai Patel, Srinivasa Iyengar and Subhas Chandra Bose.

question: What was the main reason for boycott of Simon Commission in India?
options: The President was the member of Liberal Party
explanation: Diarchy was introduced in India by the Government of India Act 1919. This Act also promised that a commission would be appointed after 10 years to review the working and progress made on the measures taken through the Act. The Simon Commission was a group of 7 MPs from Britain appointed by the British Conservative Government under Stanley Baldwin in 1927 that reached Bombay, India on February 3, 1928 to study constitutional reforms and make recommendations to the government. It was headed by Sir John Simon. It recommended a Federal form of Government. The Commission was composed entirely of British members with not a single Indian member being included in it. This was seen as an insult to Indians who were right in saying that their destiny could not be determined by a bunch of British people alone. So Indians boycotted and opposed the commission and called it ‘White Commission.’

On 26th January, 1930 for the first time in the country (under the presidency of) Jawaharlal Nehru in the Congress Lahore session, ‘Purna Swaraj Day’ was celebrated. To maintain the importance of this date, the constitution of India was adopted on 26th January 1950 and this day was declared as ‘Republic day’.

explanation: In the end of December 1929, the Indian National Congress held its annual session in the city of Lahore. The session was significant for two things: the election of Jawaharlal Nehru as President, signifying the passing of the baton of leadership to the younger generation and the proclamation of commitment to “Purna Swaraj” or Complete Independence. On December 31, 1929 Jawaharlal Nehru hoisted the flag of India’s independence on the bank of Ravi river in Lahore. In a meeting of Indian National Congress held on January 2, 1930 it was decided that ‘Complete Independence Day’ will be celebrated on January 26, 1930 and January 26 of every year will be celebrated as ‘Complete Independence Day.’

question: In which of the following Round Table Conference, the representative of the Indian National Congress participated for the first time?
explanation: On August 29, 1931, Mahatma Gandhi sailed for England in the ship ‘SS Rajputana’ to attend the Second Round Table Conference. It was for the first time when sole representative of the Indian National Congress was attending any Round Table Conference. The Conference took place in November, 1931 in London and was inconclusive, so Gandhiji returned to India and resumed civil disobedience. The new Viceroy, Lord Wellington, was deeply unsympathetic to the Indian leader. In a private letter to his sister, Willington wrote: “It’s a beautiful world if it wasn’t for Gandhi.” At the Second Round Table Conference, Mahatma Gandhi opposed the demand for separate electorates for “lower castes”. He believed that this would prevent their integration into mainstream society and permanently segregate them from other caste Hindus. The second round table conference was deemed a failure because of the many disagreements among the participants. B. R. Ambedkar opposed Mahatma Gandhi for opposing the demand for separate electorates for the Depressed Classes.

explanation: Gandhi-Irwin Pact is the name given to a political agreement concluded by Mahatma Gandhi and Lord Irwin, the then Viceroy of India, on 5th March 1931 before the Second Round Table Conference. With the efforts of Dr. M. R. Jayakar and Sir Tej Bahadur Sapru, Gandhi-Irwin Pact was signed in 1931. Terms/Features of Gandhi-Irwin Pact were as follows- (i) The Indian National Congress (INC) agreed to take part in the Round Table Conference. (ii) The Indian National Congress would stop the civil disobedience movement. (iii) Withdrawal of all ordinances that curbed the Activities of the Congress. (iv) Withdrawal of all prosecutions except those involving violent crimes. (v) Release of those who were arrested for taking part in the civil disobedience movement. (vi) Removal of the salt tax. Effects of Gandhi-Irwin Pact- (i) The Indian National Congress participated in the Second Round Table Conference which was held in 1931 during September-December. (ii) The government agreed to withdraw all ordinances. (iii) It agreed to release all political prisoners save those involved in violence. (iv) It agreed to allow peaceful picketing of liquor and foreign cloth shops. (v) It agreed to revoke the ban on the INC. (vi) It agreed to restore the confiscated properties of the Satyagrahis. (vii) It agreed to permit the collection of salt by people near the sea coasts. (viii) It agreed to forego fines not yet collected. question: Consider the following statements : 1. In the First Round Table Conference Dr. Ambedkar demanded separate electorates for the depressed classes. 2. In the Poona Pact, special provisions for representation of the depressed people in the local bodies and civil services were made. 3. The Indian National Congress did not take part in the Third Round Table Conference. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: In the First Round Table Conference (November, 1930 – January, 1931) Dr. Ambedkar demanded separate electorates for the depressed classes. He clashed with Mahatma Gandhi during the second Round Table Conference on the issue of separate electorate for depressed classes. The Indian National Congress did not take part in First and Third Round Table Conference. The Poona Pact was an agreement between Dr. Bhim Rao Ambedkar and Mahatma Gandhi signed on September 24, 1932. This pact ended Gandhi’s fast unto death. The essence of Poona Pact was more seats to depressed classes in return for their acceptance to continuance of joint electorate. Joint electorate meant that all the members of the depressed classes registered in the general electoral roll in a constituency would form an electoral college which would elect a panel of four candidates belonging to the depressed classes of the reserved seats by the method of the single vote. In the Poona Pact, special provisions for representation of the depressed people in the local bodies and civil services were made.
source: IAS (Pre) G.S. 2005 · Modern India GS p.205

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Who was directly associated to the Poona Pact of 1932?
explanation: Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, who organised the dalits into the Depressed Classes Association in 1930, clashed with Mahatma Gandhi at the Second Round Table Conference by demanding separate electorates for dalits (depressed classes/untouchables). On August 16, 1932 Ramsay Macdonald (the then Prime Minister of England) announced Communal Award which authorised Muslims, Europeans, Indian Christians, Sikhs and depressed classes (untouchables) separate electorates. In response to this Mahatma Gandhi began fast unto death in Yervada Jail on September 20, 1932. At last an agreement called ‘Poona Pact’ was signed on September 24, 1932 between Gandhi and B. R. Ambedkar and on the basis of two provisions the demand of separate electorates was accepted. Accordingly, 148 seats in different Provincial Legislatures were reserved for the Depressed Classes in place of 71 as provided in the Communal Award and in Central Legislature 18% of the seats allotted to the general electorate for British India were reserved for depressed classes. Congress agreed that adequate representation would be given to the depressed classes in the civil services. History of Modern India
source: UPPCS (Pre) G.S. 2007 · Modern India GS p.209

explanation: The Indian States committee appointed a committee under the chairmanship of Sir Harcourt Butler which was popularly known as the Butler Committee to investigate and clarify the relationship between the paramount power and Princes of Princely States in 1927 AD. Committee visited 16 states and submitted its report in 1929. The committee was formed by Lord Irwin. The following recommendations were given by the Butler committee. (i) Paramountcy must remain supreme and must fulfill its obligations, adopting and defining itself according to the shifting necessities of time amid progressive development of states. (ii) The states were bound by treaties with the Crown and the states should not be handed over without the ruler’s prior consent to an Indian Government in British India responsible to an Indian Legislature. (iii) The Viceroy, not the Governor-General in council was to be the Crown agent in dealing states.

question: The Congress in Travancore launched a Civil Disobedience Movement against the autocratic Government of the Diwan of Travancore State, who was-
explanation: The struggle for responsible government had been launched in Travancore and Cochin by 1938-39. The struggle in Cochin was far less in intensity than that in Travancore because the rulers of Cochin adopted on the whole, a lenient policy of political concessions which averted violent clashes. In June 1938, a diarchal form of Government was established allowing popular ministers to control some departments. This did not work and the Cochin Praja Mandalam was founded in 1941 to spearhead the agitation to fulfill the responsibility of the government. The Travancore State Congress launched a campaign seeking dismissal of the Diwan, C. P. Ramaswamy Iyer, against whom they had leveled certain charges. The State Congress and the Youth League were banned. The State Congress then organized a Civil Disobedience Movement. The rising tempo of the movement forced the government to withdraw the ban. The Diwan refused to open negotiation until the charges were withdrawn. The charges were finally withdrawn following Gandhiji's intervention. This created a split in the Congress. The members of the Youth League left the State Congress to join the Communist Party.

explanation: In March 1942, a mission headed by Stafford Cripps was sent to India with constitutional proposals to seek Indian support for the war. The main proposals of the Cripps mission were as follows: An Indian Union with a dominion status would be set up; it would be free to decide its relations with the Commonwealth and free to participate in the United Nations and other international bodies. After the end of the war, a constituent assembly would be convened to frame a new constitution. Members of this assembly would be partly elected by the provincial assemblies through proportional representation and partly nominated by the princes. (Hence, Statement 1 is incorrect). History of Modern India 22 s Mission and Quit India Movement The British government would accept the new constitution subject to two conditions: (i) any province not willing to join the Union could have a separate constitution and form a separate Union, and (ii) the new constitution- making body and the British government would negotiate a treaty to effect the transfer of power and to safeguard racial and religious minorities. question: Consider the following statements: The Cripps Proposals included the provision for 1. Full independence for India 2. Creation of Constitution making body. Which of the statements given above is are correct?
explanation: The Cripps Mission was sent by the British government to India in March 1942 to obtain Indian cooperation for the British war efforts in the Second World War. It was headed by Sir Richard Stafford Cripps, a Labour Minister in Winston Churchill’s coalition government in Britain. The proposals of Cripps Mission were as follows- (i) Setting up of an Indian dominion. This dominion would have the freedom to remain with the British Commonwealth or to secede from it. It would also be at liberty to take part in international organizations. (ii) A Constituent Assembly would be formed to frame a new constitution for the country. This Assembly would have members elected by the provincial assemblies and also nominated by the princes. (iii) Any province unwilling to join the Indian dominion could form a separate union and have a separate constitution. (iv) The transfer of power and the rights of minorities would be safeguarded by negotiations between the Constituent Assembly and the British government. (v) In the meantime until this new constitution came into force, India's defence would be controlled by the British and the powers of the Governor- General would remain unaltered.

question: After Quit India Movement, C. Rajagopalachari issued a pamphlet entitled “The Way Out”. Which one of the following was a proposal in this pamphlet?
options: The establishment of a "War Advisory Council" composed of representatives of British India and the Indian States.
Reconstitution of the Central Executive Council in such a way that all its members, except the Governor General and the Commander-in- Chief should be Indian leaders.
Fresh elections to the Central and Provincial Legislatures to be held at the end of
A solution for the constitutional deadlock.
explanation: “The Way Out” was a pamphlet issued by C. Rajagopalachari in 1944 to solve political deadlock between Indian National Congress and Muslim League. It is also known as C.R. Formula or C. Rajagopalachari’s Formula of 1944. The core principle of the C. R. Formula was a proposal for the Congress to offer the League the Muslim Pakistan based on plebiscite of all the peoples in the regions where Muslims had a majority. The main features were: (i) The Muslim league was to endorse the demand for independence for the traditional period, i.e. Muslim league would support the congress’s demand for complete freedom and then majority provinces would go to plebiscite especially north eastern provinces. (ii) At the end of war a commission would demarcate those contiguous areas in North West Frontier Province and North-East India where Muslims were in majority. (iii) The terms would be binding only in case of transfer by Britain of full power and responsibility for full governance of India. (iv) The Muslim league endorsing the congress demand for full independence and cooperating with it in forming an interim government in the transition period.
source: IAS (Pre) G.S. 2010 · Modern India GS p.233

question: Assertion (A): According to the Wavell Plan, the number of Hindu and Muslim members in the Executive Council were to be equal. Reason (R): Wavell thought that this arrangement would have avoided the partition of India. Code:
options: Both A and R are individually true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are individually true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is True but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Lord Wavell who had succeeded Lord Linlithgow as Governor-General in October, 1943, made a way out from the existing stalemate in India. He went to England for consultations in March 1945. He broadcast to the people of India the proposals of the British Government to resolve the deadlock in India on 14th June which is called Wavell Plan. It is also known as Breakdown Plan. The main aim of Wavell plan was not to prevent the partition of India, but to avoid the problem for sometime. The provisions of the Wavell Plan were as follows- (i) Formation of a new Executive Council at the centre in which all the members except the Viceroy and the Commander-in-Chief would be Indian. (ii) All portfolios except Defence were to be under the control of Indian members. (iii) In the proposed Executive Council which was to have 14 members, the Muslims who constituted only about 25 % of the total population were given the right to be over represented by selecting 6 representatives.
source: IAS (Pre) G.S. 2007 · Modern India GS p.241

explanation: In June, 1945 Lord Wavell invited a conference of 21 Indian Political leaders at Shimla, the Summer Capital of British India to discuss the provision of Wavell Plan. The Wavell Plan convened to agree for Indian self-government which incorporated separate representation to Muslims and reduced majority powers for both communities in their majority regions. Discussion was stuck at a point of selection of Muslim representatives. Jinnah said that no non-league Muslim should be represented to the Executive Council because only Muslim League has right to represent the Muslims of India whereas Congress said that they had no right to nominate any Muslim in the Executive council. Wavell had given place to 6 Muslims in the Executive Council of 14, and British had given it the power of Veto to any constitutional proposal which was not in its interest. But Muslims represented only 25% of Indian Population. Thus, these unreasonable demands were rejected by Congress. The Muslim league did not relent and Wavell dropped the plan. The conference was attended by the then President of Indian National Congress Maulana Abul Kalam Azad, leader of Muslim League Mohammad Ali Jinnah and other leaders of Nationalist Party, leaders of Schedule Tribes, Sikhs etc. Lord Wavell was the Viceroy of India during this period. Such provinces who left their some powers in the favour of centre, the remaining powers they would have themselves and use them in their favour. • The Representatives of Provincial Legislative Assembly and Native Princely states selected a Constituent Assembly. Seats are allotted according to the ratio of population (Generally one Representative in 10 lakhs) to the provinces. • The demand of Muslim League was denied on the basis of that, by this there would be no solution of minorities. • Provinces are divided in three categories i.e. A, B and C A – Bihar, Bombay, Middle Province, Madras, Odisha and United Province. explanation: Cripps Mission – March, 1942, C. R. Formula – July 10, 1944, Wavell Plan – June 14, 1945, Cabinet Mission – March 1946. Hence it is clear that the last opportunity to avoid the partition was lost with the rejection of Cabinet Mission. The Cabinet Mission of 1946 came to India aimed to discuss the transfer of power from the British government to the Indian leadership, with the aim of preserving India's unity and granting it independence. It is worth notable that the Cabinet Mission was composed of three Cabinet Ministers of England, Sir Pethick Lawrence (Secretary of State for India), Sir Stafford Cripps (President of the Board of Trade) and Alexander (the First Lord of the Admiralty). The mission arrived in Delhi on March 24, 1946.

explanation: Between March and May of 1947, Mountbatten decided that the Cabinet Mission Plan had become untenable and formulated an alternative plan. This plan envisaged the transfer of power to separate provinces (or to a confederation, if formed before the transfer). Punjab and Bengal were given the option to vote for partition of their provinces. The various units thus formed along with the princely states (rendered independent by lapse of paramountcy) would have the option of joining India or Pakistan or remaining separate. The plan was quickly abandoned after Nehru reacted violently to it. It is worth notable that the Plan Balkan was completed and presented on April 15-16, 1947 by Hastings Ismay, to assembly of provincial governors in Delhi. Due to this, this plan was also called “Ismay Plan”.
source: IAS (Pre) G.S. 2000 · Modern India GS p.251

It is worth notable that the British Prime Minister Clement Attlee announced on February 20, 1947 in the House of Commons that he wish to transfer powers to India but also said that if the decision related to the constitution is not made within a definite time period then the British Government has the power to transfer the government to any of them.

The idea behind the Radcliffe Line was to create a boundary which would divide India along religious demographics, under which Muslim majority provinces would become part of the new nation of Pakistan and Hindu and Sikh majority provinces would remain in India. It is worth notable that Viceroy of British India, Mountbatten has formed two commissions, Punjab Border Commission and Bengal Border Commission to decide borderline between India and Pakistan on June 30, 1947 under the Presidentship of Radcliffe. The secretary of state was a member of the British cabinet and was responsible ultimately to the British Parliament. question: Which one of the following provisions was NOT made in the Charter Act of 1833?
options: The trading Authority of the East India Company were to be abolished
The designation of the supreme authority was to be changed as the Governor-General of India in Council
All law-making powers to be conferred on Governor-General in Council
An Indian was to be appointed as a Law Member in the Governor-General’s Council History of Modern India
explanation: The Charter Act of 1833 was passed in the British Parliament which renewed the East India Company’s charter for another 20 years. This was also called the Government of India Act 1833 or the Saint Helena Act 1833. As per the provisions of this Act, the Governor-General of Bengal was re-designated as the Governor-General of India. This made Lord William Bentinck the first Governor-General of India. All financial and administrative powers were centralized in the hands of Governor General-in-Council. The number of the members of the Governor General’s council was again fixed to 4, which had been reduced by the Pitt’s India Act 1784. However, certain limits were imposed on the functioning of the 4th member. For example, the 4th member was not entitled to act as a member of the council except for legislative purposes. For the first, this fourth member of the council was Lord Macaulay. India’s first law commission was set up under Charter Act of 1833 and Lord Macaulay was made its Chairman. The Indian Councils Act 1909 empowered the viceroy to nominate one Indian member to the executive council leading to the appointment of Satyendra Prasad Sinha as the Indian member.
source: IAS (Pre) G.S. 2003 · Modern India GS p.268

question: During the period of National Movement, the incident which sowed the seeds of difference and ultimately partitioned the country was- History of Modern India
options: Reservation of separate electorate areas and places for Muslims in the Legislative Assemblies
explanation: The Indian Councils Act commonly known as Morley-Minto Reforms passed by the British Parliament in 1909 provided separate electorate for Muslims in Legislative Assemblies. This was for the first time that, the seats in the legislative bodies were reserved on the basis of religion for Muslims. Separate constituencies were marked for the Muslims and only Muslim community members were given the right to elect their representatives. The separate electorate for Muslims had a long lasting impact on India’s polity. It recognized the Muslim community as a separate section of the India and triggered the cancer of Hindu-Muslim disharmony which ultimately culminated in the partition. Under the separate electorates, Muslims could vote exclusively for the Muslim candidates in constituencies specially reserved for them. The idea was to establish that the political, economic and cultural interests of the Hindus and Muslims were distinct. The unity between Hindus and Muslims is a illusion and this Act sowed the seeds of the Communalism. This incident sowed the seeds of difference and ultimately partitioned the country.
source: UPPCS (Pre) G.S. 2003 UPPCS (Pre) Spl. G.S. 2004 · Modern India GS p.269

They contained provisions that ensured that British officials retained their majority in the Imperial Legislative Council. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: The Indian Councils Act 1909 or Morley- Minto Reforms was passed by British Parliament in 1909 in an attempt to widen the scope of legislative councils, placate the demands of moderates in Indian National Congress and to increase the participation of Indians in the governance. This Act got royal assent on 25 May 1909. Lord Morley was Secretary of State of India in England and Lord Minto was the Viceroy of India. The Act introduced separate and discriminatory electorate. The Act contained provisions that ensured that British officials retained their majority in the Imperial Legislative Council.

options: It introduced parliamentary supervision over the East India Company.

It changed the power of vote in the Court of Proprietors by removing all restrictions on qualifications.
The Governor-General was vested with a casting vote.
explanation: The Regulating Act was passed in the British Parliament in June 1773. It was the first parliamentary ratification and authorization defining the powers and authority of the East India Company with respect to its Indian possessions. The provisions of Regulating Act of 1773 were as follows- (i) It introduced parliamentary supervision over the East India Company. (ii) It designated the Governor-General of Bengal and created an Executive Council of four members to assist him. Lord Warren Hastings was the first Governor-General of Bengal and Governors of Bombay and Madras presidencies subordinate to the Governor-General of Bengal. (iii) The Governor General was vested with a casting vote.
source: UPSC CAPF G.S. Ist 2014 · Modern India GS p.272

question: By which Act Bihar became a separate state?
explanation: When it got separated from the Bengal Presidency in 1912, Bihar and Orissa comprised a single province. Later, under the Government of India Act of 1935, the division of Orissa became a separate province and the province of Bihar came into being as an administrative unit of British India. After Independence in 1947, the State of Bihar, with the same geographic boundary, formed a part of the Republic of India, until 1956. At that time, an area in the south-east, predominantly the district of Purulia, was separated and incorporated into West Bengal as part of the linguistic reorganization of Indian States.

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Who among the following were the founders of the "Hind Mazdoor Sabha" established in 1948?
options: B. Krishna Pillai, E.M.S. Namboodiripad and K.C. George
Jayaprakash Narayan, Deen Day al Upadhyay and M.N. Roy
C.P. Ramaswamy Iyer, K. Kamaraj and Veeresalingam Pantulu
Ashok Mehta, T.S. Ramanujam and G.G. Mehta
explanation: The Hind Mazdoor Sabha (HMS) is a National Trade Union Centre in India. It was founded in Howrah on December 24, 1948 by Socialist Forward Bloc followers and independent unionists. Its founders included Basawan Singh (Sinha), Ashok Mehta, R. S. Ruikar, Mani Benkara, Shibnath Benarjee, R. K. Khedgikar, T. S. Ramanujam, V. S. Mathur and G. G. Mehta. Mr. R. S. Ruikar was elected as the President and Ashok Mehta as its General Secretary. The HMS absorbed the Indian Federation of Labour and the Socialist Hind Mazdoor Panchayat. The Hind Mazdoor Sabha was intended to be a third force in Indian trade unionism, balancing between INTUC on one side and AITUC on the other. INTUC was discarded because it was believed to be under the control of the government and AITUC was rejected because it was controlled by the Communist Party.
source: IAS (Pre) G.S. 2018 · Modern India GS p.279

explanation: The British Indian Association was established on October 31, 1851. The first committee of the association was composed of Raja Radhakanta Deb – President, Raja Kalikrishna Deb – Vice-President, Debendranath Tagore – Secretary, Digambar Mitra – Asst. Secretary. In May 1884, M. Veeraraghavachariar, G. Subramania Iyer and P. Anandacharlu established the Madras Mahajana Sabha. Gazulu Lakshminarasu Chetty was an Indian merchant, Indian Independence activist and political activist who founded the Madras Native Association. Indian association was the first declared nationalist organization founded in British India by Surendranath Banerjee and Anand Mohan Bose in 1876 AD.
source: IAS (Pre) G.S. 2017 · Modern India GS p.279

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Who was the founder of Indian Association?
explanation: Indian National Association was the first declared Nationalist organization founded in British India by Surendranath Banerjee and Anand Mohan Bose in July, 1876. It favoured local self-government and served as a preparatory agent for the more truly Indian National Congress. The association found an issue in opposing the lowering of the age limit for civil service examinations (1877), which was disadvantageous to Indian candidates; and in 1878 it objected to the Vernacular Press Act, which stifled the Indian press. After the Indian National Congress was founded in 1885, the association gradually lost ground; it was not heard of after 1888.

The schools and hospitals of the Mission are rendering yeomen service. Through his efforts at a cultural resurgence, Swami Vivekananda laid strong foundations for the nationalist movement. He introduced Covenant Civil Services (Higher Civil Services) which were different from the Un-covenanted Civil Services (Lower Civil Services). After being the Governor-General of Bengal, Cornwallis restructured the administration and abolished the revenue boards and laid the fresh laws for them. He divided the jurisdiction of civil and judicial administration through ‘Cornwallis Code’ which later changed into Civil Services in India. Charter Act of 1853 abolished the patronage system and introduced the system of open competition as the basis of selection of Civil Services. Surendra Nath Banerjee was the first to clear the ICS (Indian Civil Service) examinations. Though he passed the ICS in 1869 AD, he was dismissed because of a dispute over his correct age. After this matter was sorted out in a court of law, Banerjee reappeared for the exam and once again managed to clear it in 1871 AD. He was appointed as the Assistant Magistrate in Sylhet, but was chucked out due to racial discrimination. While Subhash Chandra Bose resigned after passing the examination.

question: The Ilbert Bill controversy was related to the-
options: imposition of restrictions on the Indians of certain to carry arms by Indians
imposition of restrictions on newspapers and magazines published in Indian languages
removal of disqualifications imposed on the Indian magistrates with regard to the trial of the Europeans
removal of a duty on imported cotton cloth
explanation: Ilbert Bill was named after Courtenay Peregrine Ilbert, who was appointed as legal adviser to the Council of India. The bill was introduced in 1883 by the then Viceroy Lord Ripon, who actually desired to abolish the racial prejudice from the Indian Penal Code. Ripon had proposed an amendment for existing laws in the country and to allow Indian judges and magistrates the jurisdiction to prosecute British offenders in criminal cases at the District level. It was never allowed before. So naturally, the Europeans living in India looked it as a humiliation and the introduction of the bill led to intense opposition in Britain as well as India (by the British residents). So it was withdrawn but was reintroduced and enacted in 1884 in a severely compromised state.

question: Which Governor-General introduced the Civil Services for the first time in India?
explanation: Charles Cornwallis reformed and implemented the Civil Service system in India. Cornwallis introduced two divisions of the Indian Civil Service namely, covenanted and uncovenanted. The covenanted civil service consisted of only Europeans that comprised the British personnel occupying the higher posts in the government. The uncovenanted civil service was solely aimed at and introduced to facilitate the entry of Indians at the subordinate posts of the administration. He is known as the father of civil services in India.

question: The Indian Public Service was enforced during the period of-
explanation: Lord Cornwallis twice held the high post of Governor-General. His first tenure lasted from 1786 AD to 1793 AD. For second time, he came to India in 1805 AD, but died before he could do any wonders again. Lord Cornwallis was the first English nobleman to come to India to undertake the office of the Governor General and also the first of Parliamentary Governor Generals of India. He was also the first Governor General to die in India (during his second term). He created Civil Service in India. He introduced a new revenue system under the Permanent Settlement of Bengal in 1793 AD with a view to stabilize land revenue and create a loyal contented class of Zamindars. To curb the corruption in the company, Cornwallis was given sufficient powers and authorities. He put in place the rules and regulations for the servants of the Company. He exclusively divided the jurisdiction of civil and judicial administration through “Cornwallis Code” which later transformed into Civil Services in India. He set up courts in the states, districts and provinces. So far Police was under the Zamindars. It was taken away from Zamindars and handed over to the Superintendent of the Police at District level. The Police was Europeanized and were now paid salary and given unlimited powers to arrest the suspected persons.
source: UPPCS (Mains) Spl. 2004 · Modern India GS p.295

explanation: The Regulating Act was passed during the regime of Lord Warren Hastings in 1773 AD. It was the first parliamentary ratification and authorization defining the powers and authority of the East India Company with respect to its Indian possessions. The Act provided for appointment of a Governor-General along with four Councilors in the Presidency of Fort William (Calcutta), jointly called the Governor-General in Council. As per this, Warren Hastings was appointed as the Governor-General of the Presidency of Fort William. The Governors in Councils at Madras and Bombay were brought under the control of Bengal, especially in matters of foreign policy. Now, they could not wage war against Indian states without Bengal’s approval. Lord Cornwallis introduced the Permanent Settlement. The Annexation of Sindh took place in 1843 AD during the reign of Governor-General Lord Ellenborough (1842-44 AD). The First Afghan War (1838-42 AD) took place during the reign of Lord Auckland (1836-42 AD).

explanation: The then British Prime Minister Gladstone sent Lord Ripon as Viceroy of India in 1880 AD. Ripon was liberal in his attitude and made some remarkable changes in the administrative system of India. To improve the lot of the factory workers in towns, he passed the first Factory Act in 1881 AD. The Act prohibited the employment of children under the age of seven years, limited the number of working hours for children below the age of twelve years and required that dangerous machinery should be fenced properly. Lord Ripon is also remembered for his attempts to establish local self-government in 1882 AD. He is considered to be the ‘Father of Local Self-Government.’ History of Modern India

question: Who among the following was related to the policy of ‘Masterly Inactivity’?
explanation: Lord John Lawrence served as the Viceroy of India from 1864 AD to 1869 AD. The policy of ‘Masterly Inactivity’ was followed by the British against Afghanistan from 1860 AD to 1876 AD. It was conceived by Lord John Lawrence. The policy of Masterly Inactivity was opposed to the policy of misdirected war and activity. As long as Russia was out of Afghanistan, the British remained inactive in Afghan affairs. It is worth notable that the policies of Lord Elgin (1862-63), Lord Lawrence (1864-69), Lord Mayo (1869-72) and Lord Northbrook (1872-76) are collectively called the period of Policy of Masterly Inactivity. The main objective of the British policy during this period was let things go quietly on to give the land rest. It was opposite to the “Forward Policy” of Lord Lytton.

explanation: Replacing Lord Auckland in 1842 AD, Lord Ellenborough came to India as Governor-General and in the same year he appointed Charles James Napier as Major General of British Army replacing Major Outram. The Battle of Miani was a battle between forces of the Bombay Army of the British East India Company under Charles Napier and the Baluch Army of Talpur Amirs of Sindh, led by Mir Nasir Khan Talpur. The battle took place in 1843 AD at Miani, Sindh. This battle eventually led to the capture of parts of Sindh region, first territorial possession by British East India Company. The whole of Sindh was annexed in British India in 1843 AD and the Amirs of Sind, their kith and kin were taken prisoners and then these broken-hearted and miserable men were sent to Burma in exile. Note:- Baluchi Chiefs were collectively known as “Amirs of Sindh.”

He said “There we find the same attempt at a rule excessively centralized and intensely personal, the same strenuous purpose, the same overpowering consciousness of duty, the same persistence in a policy of distrust and repression, resulting in bitter exasperation all round”. Gokhale said that Lord Curzon did not understand India, he thought India was a country where Englishmen were to monopolize all power.

The war ended with the signing of History of Modern India 30 the Treaty of Sugauli in 1816, which ceded some Nepalese controlled territory to the British. As per the treaty, Nepal lost all Sikkim (including Darjeeling), the territories of Kumaon and Garhwal and Western Terai region.

question: Dalhousie has been regarded as the maker of modern India because he brought about reforms and made a beginning in many fields. Which one among the following was not one of his schemes of reforms?
options: Construction of railways and introduction of telegraph and postal services
Establishment of a public works department
Factories Act to improve the condition of Indian labour
explanation: Lord Dalhousie was the Governor-General of India from 1848 AD to 1856 AD. He was responsible for introducing a variety of modern reforms such as the railways, telegraph and postal networks, and public works in India. The Factories Act was passed in 1881 AD during the regime of Lord Ripon. The Act prohibited the employment of children under the age of seven years, limited the number of working hours for children below the age of twelve years and required that dangerous machinery should be fenced properly. The Act also made provision for one hour rest during the working period and four days leave in a month for the workers. Inspectors were appointed to supervise the implementation of these measures.

subject: AP & Indian History
question: The Vital-Vidhvansak, the first monthly journal to have the untouchable people as its target audience was published by____.
explanation: Gopal Baba Walangkar was an activist who worked to release the untouchable people of India from their historic socio-economic oppression. He developed a racial theory to explain the oppression and also published the first journal targeted at the untouchable people. In 1888, Walangkar began publishing the monthly journal titled Vital-Vidhvansak.
source: UPSC IAS (Pre) 2020 · Modern India GS p.312

subject: AP & Indian History
question: With reference to the book “Desher Katha” written by Sakharam Ganesh Deuskar during the freedom struggle, consider the following statements: 1. It warned against the Colonial State’s hypnotic conquest of the mind 2. It inspired the performance of swadeshi street plays and folk songs. 3. The use of ‘desh’ by Deuskar was in the specific context of the region of Bengal. Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation: Sakharam Ganesh Deuskar published a book entitled 'Desher Katha' describing in exhaustive detail of the British commercial and industrial exploitation of India. Sakharam Ganesh Deuskar popularized the ideas of Naoroji and Ranade and promoted swadeshi in a popular idiom. It inspired swadeshi street plays and folk songs and had become a mandatory text for an entire generation of swadeshi activists.
source: UPSC IAS (Pre) 2020 · Modern India GS p.312

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Who started the newspaper "Indian Sociologist" abroad?
explanation: Shyamji Krishna Varma was an Indian revolutionary fighter, an India patriot, lawyer and journalist who founded the Indian Home Rule Society, India House and The Indian Sociologist in London. • In 1905, he founded the India House and the Indian Sociologist, which rapidly developed as and organised meeting point for radical nationalists among Indian students in Britain at the time and one of the most prominent centres for revolutionary Indian nationalism outside India.

question: Who was the author of the book "The Problems of the East"?
explanation: The book 'The Problems of the East' was written by Lord Curzon. It was published in 1894. The book presents a contemporary condition of Japan, Korea and China within a changing international landscape.
source: OPSC (OCS)-2018 Paper-I · Modern India GS p.313

subject: AP & Indian History
question: The editor of the paper "Hindu Patriot", Sri Harishchandra Mukherjee was known to have helped the:
explanation: The Hindu Patriot under the able editorship of Harish Chandra Mukherjee became the mouthpiece of protest against imperial injustices. In the late fifties, the Hindu Patriot began to expose the oppression and atrocities on Indian peasants by the indigo planters. Latter used to force the peasants into cultivating indigo. • In the late 1895 after the initial editorship of Girish Chandra Ghosh and Harish Chandra Mukherjee. Krishnadas Pal was the editor of the paper for 23 years. During the period he opposed the imperial laws like the Immigration Bill, the Vernacular Press Act and the Illbert Bill through the Columns of the Hindu Patriot.
source: OPSC (OCS)-2018 Paper-I · Modern India GS p.313

subject: AP & Indian History
question: The official historian of India’s struggle for independence was-
explanation: Dr. S. N. Sen was the official historian of India’s Struggle for Independence. He believed that the uprising of 1857 was a war of Independence. He contends that revolutions are mostly the work of a minority, with or without the active sympathy of the masses. Such was the case with the American Revolution of 1775- 1783 and the French Revolution. Dr. Sen contends that when a rebellion can claim the sympathies of the substantial majority of the population, it can claim a national character. Dr. Sen comes to the conclusion that “The mutiny became a revolt and assumed a political character when the mutineers of Meerut placed themselves under the king of Delhi and a section of the landed aristocracy and civil population declared in his favour what began as a fight for religion ended as war of Indecent for there is not the slightest doubt that the rebels wanted to get rid of the alien government and restore the old order of which the king of Delhi was the rightful representative”. According to Dr. Sen, the struggle may be described as "a war of fanatic religionists against Christians".
source: UPPCS (Pre) G.S. 2010 · Modern India GS p.324

explanation: The Vande Mataram was an Indian nationalist publication from Paris which began in September, 1909 by the Paris Indian Society. explanation: After the Second Round Table Conference, British government agreed to give Communal Award to the Depressed Classes on the request of B. R. Ambedkar. Gandhi opposed the government's decision which he considered it would divide the Hindu society and subsequently went on to the indefinite fast in Yerwada Jail. He ended his fast after signing Poona Pact with Ambedkar on September 25, 1932. On September 30, 1932 Gandhi founded All India Anti Untouchability League, to remove untouchability in the society, which later renamed as Harijan Sevak Sangh (Servants of Untouchables Society). explanation: The British Indian Association was founded after amalgamating the “Landholders Society” and “British India Society” on October 31, 1851. This was the first political organization that brought the Indians together. The President of the first committee of this organization was Raja Radhakanta Deb, while Debendranath Tagore was its Secretary. The newspaper of this society was “Hindu Patriot” which was the first newspaper published by an Indian in English language. Its editor was Harish Chandra Mukherjee. He was associated with the Hindu Patriot right from its starting in 1853 and in 1855 he secured the ownership and became the editor of the newspaper. Harish Chandra Mukherjee played a vital pioneering role in Indigo Movement with his brilliant writing in the Hindu Patriot. His writing roused public opinion and finally Dinabandhu Mitra came out with his play Nil Darpan in 1860.

explanation: Shom Prakash was started by Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar in 1859. Iswar Chandra Vidyasagar proposed the publication of a weekly newspaper Som Prakash partly with the objective of providing employment for a deaf scholar. explanation: Lectures from Colombo to Almora (1897) is a book of Swami Vivekananda based on his various lectures. After visiting the West, Vivekananda reached Colombo, British Ceylon (now Sri Lanka) in January 1897. Upon Vivekananda's arrival in South India a 40 feet high monument was built by the king of Ramnad on the spot where he landed to celebrate his achievements at the West. He reached Calcutta via Madras on January 20, 1897. Then Vivekananda travelled extensively and visited many Indian states. On June 19, 1897 he reached Almora. The lectures delivered by him in this period were compiled into the book-Lectures from Colombo to Almora. The book contains reports of his 17 lectures.
source: IAS (Pre) G.S. 2006 · Modern India GS p.329

The story is set in the backdrop of Pathan- Mughal conflicts that took place in south-western region of modern-day Indian state of West Bengal during the reign of Akbar.

explanation: The report ‘Journey through the Kingdom of Oudh in the year 1849-50’ was authored by W. H. Sleeman. Born in 1788 W.H. Sleeman came to India as an infantry cadet in the Bengal army in 1809. He rose through the rank finally to become Major-General in 1854. He is best remembered for his work for the suppression of the Thugs.
source: UPPCS (Mains) G.S. Ist 2013 · Modern India GS p.330

subject: AP & Indian History
question: The author of the book ‘The Man Who Divided India’ was-
options: Larry Collins and Dominique Lapierre History of Modern India
explanation: The author of the book ‘The Man Who Divided India’ was Rafiq Zakaria while Abul Kalam Azad wrote ‘India Wins Freedom’, Dr. Rajendra Prasad wrote ‘India Divided’ and Larry Collins and Dominique Lapierre authored ‘Freedom at Mid Night’.
source: UPPCS (Pre) G.S. 2014 · Modern India GS p.330

subject: AP & Indian History
question: The editor of ‘Swadeshwahini’ was-
explanation: The editor of ‘Swadeshwahini’ was K. Ramakrishna Pillai.
source: UPPCS (Pre) G.S. 2005 · Modern India GS p.330

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Who among the following wrote about Home Land of Aryans?
explanation: 'The Arctic Home in the Vedas' is a book on the origin of Aryans by Lokmanya Bal Gangadhar Tilak. The book was written at the end of 1898 but was first published in March 1903 in Pune. It propounded the theory that the North Pole was the original home of Aryans during pre-glacial period which they had to leave due to the ice deluge around 8000 B.C. and had to migrate to the Northern part of Europe and Asia in search of lands for new settlements. In support to his theory, Tilak has presented certain Vedic hymns, East Iranian passages, Vedic chronology and Vedic calendars with interpretations of the contents in detail.
source: UPPCS (Pre) G.S. 1996 · Modern India GS p.330

subject: AP & Indian History
question: The memoir entitled 'Bapu : My Mother' was written by-
explanation: The memoir entitled ‘Bapu: My Mother’ was written by Kumari Manuben Gandhi.
source: UPPCS (Mains) G.S. Ist 2013 · Modern India GS p.330

subject: AP & Indian History
question: The pamphlet entitled ‘Why I am an Atheist?' was written by-
explanation: ‘Why I am an Atheist’ is an essay written by Indian revolutionary Bhagat Singh in 1930 in Lahore Central Jail. The essay was a reply to his religious friends who thought Bhagat Singh became an atheist because of his vanity.
source: UPPCS (Mains) G.S. Ist 2010 · Modern India GS p.330

subject: AP & Indian History
question: The book 'India's Struggle for Independence' was authored by-
explanation: The book ‘India’s Struggle for Independence’ was authored by Bipin Chandra.
source: UPPCS (Mains) G.S. Ist 2010 · Modern India GS p.330

subject: AP & Indian History
question: The book "Mountbatten and the Partition of India" was written by:
explanation: The imperialist historian Larry Collins and Dominic Lapierre wrote the book 'Mountbatten and the Partition of India' based on the partition of India in which Mountbatten was not convicted for the partition of India.
source: UPPCS (Mains) G.S. Ist 2009 · Modern India GS p.331

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Who was the author of the book 'Bandi Jivan'?
explanation: The author of the book ‘Bandi Jivan’ (in Hindi and Gurumukhi) is Sachindra Sanyal. The book mostly attracted youngsters towards revolution. It is worth notable that Sachindra Sanyal along with Chandra Shekhar Azad and Ram Prasad Bismil founded Hindustan Republic Association (HRA) in October, 1924 at Kanpur.
source: UPPCS (Mains) G.S. Ist 2007 · Modern India GS p.331

subject: AP & Indian History
question: The book ‘Mother India’ was written by-
explanation: The polemical book ‘Mother India’ was authored by American historian Katherine Mayo while Lala Lajpat Rai wrote ‘Unhappy India’. Bal Gangadhar Tilak published ‘Kesari’ and Bipin Chandra Pal wrote ‘The Soul of India’ and ‘Memories of My Life and Times’.
source: UPPCS (Mains) G.S. Ist 2006 · Modern India GS p.331

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Who wrote the famous song 'Saare Jahan Se Achcha Hindustan Hamara'?
explanation: The renowned poet and lawyer by profession, Muhammad Iqbal wrote “Saare Jahan Se Achcha Hindustan Hamara”.
source: UPPCS (Mains) G.S. Ist 2004 · Modern India GS p.331

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Who among the following was official historian of Congress?
explanation: The official historian of Congress was Pattabhi Sitaramaiyya. The name of the book was ‘History of Congress’. History of Modern India
source: Uttarakhand PSC (Pre) G.S. 2002-03 · Modern India GS p.331

subject: AP & Indian History
question: The author of ‘Bharat-Bharti’ is-
explanation: The author of ‘Bharat Bharti’ is Maithili Sharan Gupt. The book has been written in Husaddas Hali (a form of Urdu poem) genre. Gupt entered the world of Hindi literature by writing poems in various magazines, including Saraswati. In 1910, his first major work, ‘Rang mein Bhang’ was published by Indian Press. With ‘Bharat Bharati’ his nationalist poems became popular among Indians, who were struggling for independence. His other works include Saket, Yashodhara etc.
source: Uttarakhand UDA/LDA (Pre) 2006 · Modern India GS p.331

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Who is the author of the book named ‘Landmarks in Indian Constitutional and National Development’?
explanation: The First Governor of Rajasthan Gurumukh Nihal Singh wrote the book ‘Landmarks in Indian Constitutional and National Development’. It was published in 1950 from Delhi.
source: Uttarakhand UDA/LDA (Pre) 2006 · Modern India GS p.331

subject: AP & Indian History
question: The writer of ‘Indian National Movement : The Long Term Dynamics’ is-
explanation: The author of ‘Indian National Movement: The Long Term Dynamics’ is Bipin Chandra.
source: UP Lower (Pre) G.S. 2015 · Modern India GS p.331

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Which Urdu newspaper was started by Lala Lajpat Rai in 1920 from Lahore?
explanation: Lala Lajpat Rai started ‘Vande Mataram’ in 1920 from Lahore. It is worth notable that he also presided the annual session of Indian National Congress held in Calcutta in 1920.
source: UP Lower Spl. (Pre) 2008 · Modern India GS p.331

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Which of the following was conferred with the honour of 'National Poet' for contributing to the freedom struggle by his literary works?
explanation: Maithili Sharan Gupt was conferred with the honour of ‘National Poet’ for contributing to the freedom struggle by his literary works. At the time of freedom movement, he filled up the new empowered agitators through his ardent writings.
source: UP Lower (Pre) 2002 · Modern India GS p.331

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Who founded ‘Amrit Bazar’ magazine?
explanation: In 1868, Amrita Bazar Patrika, a Bengali daily newspaper was started by Shishir Kumar Ghosh, Moti Lal Ghosh and Tusar Kanti Ghosh. It was used as a tool to expose British agent’s cruel deeds of tyranny.
source: BPSC (Pre) G.S. 2004-05 · Modern India GS p.332

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Which among the following newspapers was mainly the propagator of policies of moderates?
explanation: The newspaper ‘Leader’ was mainly the propagator of policies of moderates. The editor of ‘Leader’ was Pandit Madan Mohan Malviya. ‘New India’ and ‘Commonweal’ was edited by Annie Besant, Mahatma Gandhi founded ‘Young India’ in 1918 while ‘Free Press Journal’ was a news agency.
source: BPSC (Pre) 2004-05 · Modern India GS p.332

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Who wrote ‘Jhanda Geet’?
explanation: ‘Jhanda Geet’ was written by Shyamlal Gupta ‘Parshad’ while he was in Kanpur Jail in 1924.
source: BPSC (Pre) G.S. 2003-04 · Modern India GS p.332

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Who started the newspaper ‘Free Hindustan’ in America?
explanation: In 1905, Tarankanath Das sailed to Japan and lived there in exile under an assumed name Tarak Brahmachari and after one year he went to San Francisco, USA and launched his journal named “Free Hindustan” from Vancouver, America in April, 1908. With its columns he started influencing the American public opinion about the real condition of India and circulated the cause of a free Indian republic. He established the Indian Independence League in California and also helped Lala Hardayal in organizing the Ghadar Party Movement in the USA.
source: BPSC (Pre) G.S. 1994 · Modern India GS p.332

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Who was the author of ‘Indian Unrest’?
options: Valentine Chirol History of Modern India
explanation: ‘Indian Unrest’ was authored by Valentine Chirol. In his book, Valentine Chirol termed Tilak as ‘Father of Indian Unrest’.
source: BPSC (Pre) G.S. 1994 · Modern India GS p.332

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Which one of the following newspapers of pre- independence Rajasthan was not the promoter of Arya Samaj ideology?
explanation: ‘The Rajputana Gazette’ was an Urdu weekly edited by Maulavi Murad Ali from Ajmer in 1885 which did not promote the ideology of Arya Samaj. Later his wife Moti Begum operated the newspaper after his death.
source: RAS/RTS (Pre) G.S. 2016 · Modern India GS p.332

subject: AP & Indian History
question: In 1920s, with the objective of political awakening who published newspaper ‘Rajasthan’ from Beawar?
explanation: With the objective of political awakening Rishi Dutt Mehta published the newspaper ‘Rajasthan’ weekly from Beawar in 1920s.
source: RAS/RTS (Pre) G.S. 2015 · Modern India GS p.332

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Which among the following poet is called Tagore of Punjab?
explanation: Professor Puran Singh is also known as ‘Tagore of Punjab’. He was a Punjabi poet and mystic. Born in Abbottabad, now in Pakistan, in an Ahluwalia family, he is acclaimed as one of the founders of modern Punjabi poetry.
source: Jharkhand PSC (Pre) G.S. 2015 · Modern India GS p.332

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Who among the following revolutionaries wrote an article ‘An Introduction to the Dreamland’?
explanation: ‘An Introduction to the Dreamland’ is an article written by Bhagwati Charan Vohra in America which illustrated an image of independent India.
source: UP UDA/LDA Spl. (Pre) 2006 · Modern India GS p.332

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Who among the following is the biographer of Mahatma Gandhi?
explanation: Bal Ram Nanda (1917 – 2010) was a writer from New Delhi, India. He was the preeminent Indian biographer of Mahatma Gandhi. He wrote many books. One of them is Mahatma Gandhi : A biography.
source: UPPSC Food Safety Inspector Exam 2013 · Modern India GS p.332

subject: AP & Indian History
question: The editor of ‘Indian Mirror’ started in the early stages of the struggle against British rule was-
explanation: ‘Indian Mirror’ was published by Manmohan Ghosh in 1861 from Calcutta. He himself was the editor of the newspaper. Later S. N. Sen became the editor of ‘Indian Mirror’. As Manmohan Ghosh has not been mentioned in the option, hence option (d) would be considered as the correct answer.
source: UPPSC Asst. Forest Conservator Exam 2015 · Modern India GS p.333

question: The paper 'Indian Mirror' was published during 1880 from-
source: UPPCS (Mains) G.S. Ist 2007 · Modern India GS p.333

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
options: Calcutta Gazette - 1784 History of Modern India
explanation: Newspapers Establishment Year Bombay Herald - 1789 Madras Courier - 1785 Calcutta Gazette - 1784 Bengal Gazette - 1780 The Hindu - 1878 208.The first historian of 19th century who wrote about the feudal system of Rajasthan was- (a) Colonel James Tod (b) Dr. L. P. Tessitori (c) George Grearson (d) John Thomas RAS/RTS (Pre) G.S. 2009 Ans. (a): The first historian of 19th century, Colonel James Tod in his book ‘Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan’ published in 1829 used the word ‘Rajwada’, ‘Raithan’ or ‘Rajasthan’ for the state.
source: UP PSC ACF/RFO (Mains) 2020 Paper I · Modern India GS p.333

subject: AP & Indian History
question: "Majahab Nahi Sikhata Aapas Me Bair Rakhna"who wrote the following lines in his work?
explanation: “Mahajab Nahi Sikhata Aapas Me Bair Rakhna” is a part from the poem “Saare Jahan Se Achha Hindustan Hamara” which is written by Mohammad Iqbal. The poem was published in the weekly journal ‘Ittehad’ on August 16, 1904. Recited by Iqbal, the following year at Government College, Lahore, now in Pakistan. It quickly became an anthem of opposition to the British rule in India.
source: MPPSC (Pre) G.S. 1998 · Modern India GS p.333

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Which of the following statements about 'Varnaparichay’, a mid 19th century Bengali text is/are correct? 1. It was written by Raja Rammohan Roy. 2. It was the most widely used Bengali primer of the time. Select correct answer using code given below.
explanation: Varna Parichay is a primer of the Bangla language written by Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar in 1855. This was the first book designed on logical principles to teach the Bangla alphabet to the beginners systematically.
source: UPSC CAPF G.S. Ist 2016 · Modern India GS p.333

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Which among the following pairs is not correctly matched?
options: Dadabhai Naoroji : Poverty and Un-British Rule in India
Frank Moraes : India from Curzon to Nehru and After
explanation: ‘India from Curzon to Nehru and After’ was authored by Durga Das. Rest of the options are correctly matched.
source: UPPCS (Pre) G.S. 2014 · Modern India GS p.334

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Who among the following is the author of the book ‘The Social Contract’?
explanation: ‘The Social Contract’, originally published as ‘The Social Contract, or 'Principles of Political Rights’ by Jean-Jacques Rousseau, is a 1762 book in which Rousseau theorized about the best way to establish a political community in the face of the problems of commercial society, which he had already identified in his book 'Discourse on Inequality (1754)'. The Social Contract helped, inspire political reforms or revolutions in Europe, especially in France.
source: UPSC CDS IInd 2017 · Modern India GS p.334

subject: AP & Indian History
question: The famous Urdu Weekly 'Al-Hilal' was started in which of the following years?
explanation: The famous Urdu Weekly Al-Hilal was published in 1912 AD by Maulana Abul Kalam Azad.
source: UP PSC ACF/RFO (Mains) 2020 Paper I · Modern India GS p.334

subject: AP & Indian History
question: With reference to Madanapalle of Andhra Pradesh, which one of the following statements is correct?
options: Pingali Venkayya designed the tricolour Indian National Flag here.
Pattabhi Sitaramayya led the Quit India Movement of Andhra region from here.
Rabindranath Tagore translated the National Anthem from Bengali to English here.
Madame Blavatsky and Colonel Olcott set up headquarters of Theosophical Society first here.
explanation: The original song 'Jana Gana Mana' (National Anthem) was written in Bengali. The idea of translating the song from Bengali to English came to Rabindranath Tagore while he was visiting the Besant Theosophical College on the invitation of Irish poet James H. Cousins. He penned down the english translation during his stay at Madanapalle, a small town in the Chittoor district of Andhra Pradesh. Hence, option (c) is the correct answer.
source: UPSC (IAS) 2021 · Modern India GS p.334

subject: AP & Indian History
question: Who among the following is associated with 'Songs from Prison', a translation of ancient Indian religious lyrics in English?
explanation: ‘Songs from Prison' is a book of translation from Sanskrit hymns and lyrics, from the Upanishads and other scriptures. Mahatma Gandhi made these translations during his incarceration in Yerwada Prison in 1930. Translations of works by Manu, Tulsidas, Kabir, Nanak, Mirabai, Ramdas, Tukaram and many other poets. Gandhi prepared these translations mainly for his English friends and especially for Mirabehn. Hence, option (c) is the correct Answer.
source: UPSC (IAS) 2021 · Modern India GS p.334

question: Match List-I (Books) with List-II (Authors) and select the correct answer using the codes given below : List-I List-II A. My Presidential Years 1. S. Radhakrishnan B.
